title: Self-testing In Fermionic Networks
authors: Fatemeh Moradi Kalarde, Luis Mu\~{n}ecas Tom\'{a}s, Marc-Olivier Renou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-testing certifies quantum states and measurements from observed correlations alone, without assumptions on the inner workings of the devices. Its standard formulation, however, models the devices as manipulating qudits, of arbitrary or even infinite dimension. Yet febits, information encoded in the presence or absence of a fermion in a mode, can produce correlations in quantum networks that no qudit model reproduces under the same locality constraints. We first show that the modeling choice in terms of qudits or febits matters for self-testing: some correlations that self-test a unique qudit strategy admit two fermionic realizations inequivalent under local parity-preserving isometries. We then develop a fermionic self-testing framework and show that the correlations of a three-party rewiring network single out febit states and measurements up to such isometries, providing the first genuine fermionic self-test.
tldr: The paper introduces a fermionic self-testing framework and provides the first genuine fermionic self-test, showing that febit correlations in a three-party rewiring network uniquely determine fermionic states and measurements up to local parity-preserving isometries.
motivation: Standard self-testing assumes qudit models, but fermionic systems (febits) can produce correlations not reproducible by qudits under the same locality constraints, so a fermionic self-testing framework is needed.
method: The authors first demonstrate that qudit and febit modeling choices lead to inequivalent self-testing conclusions, then develop a fermionic self-testing framework using local parity-preserving isometries and apply it to a three-party rewiring network.
result: They find correlations that self-test a unique qudit strategy but admit two inequivalent fermionic realizations, and show that the three-party rewiring network's correlations single out febit states and measurements up to the relevant isometries.
conclusion: This work establishes the first genuine fermionic self-test, highlighting the necessity of fermionic models for self-testing in quantum networks and opening a new direction in device-independent certification.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses a foundational issue in quantum self-testing: the standard qudit model of devices may be inadequate when the underlying physical systems are fermionic. The authors introduce febits—two-level systems defined by the presence or absence of a fermion in a mode—and show that correlations achievable in quantum networks with febits can be impossible to reproduce with qudits under the same locality constraints. They first demonstrate that the modeling choice matters: a correlation that self-tests a unique qudit strategy admits two inequivalent fermionic realizations under local parity-preserving isometries. This implies that standard qudit-based self-testing cannot distinguish between these fermionic strategies. The authors then develop a fermionic self-testing framework, adapting the notion of isometric equivalence to respect fermionic superselection rules (parity preservation). As a key result, they show that the correlations from a three-party rewiring network—a network where fermionic modes are rewired among parties—uniquely single out febit states and measurements up to local parity-preserving isometries. This constitutes the first genuine fermionic self-test, establishing that self-testing can be extended to fermionic systems and that the qudit paradigm is insufficient for such scenarios. The work has implications for certifying quantum devices in fermionic architectures and for understanding the role of superselection rules in quantum information.

The fermionic self-testing framework is built by adapting the standard self-testing definition: instead of requiring equivalence up to arbitrary local isometries, they require equivalence up to local isometries that commute with the parity operator. The key technical tool is the three-party rewiring network, where fermionic modes are distributed and rewired among parties. The authors analyze the resulting correlations and prove that they uniquely determine the febit states and measurements up to the allowed isometries. title: Convex Splitting By Binary Quantum Hypothesis Testing
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from [MATH] independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by [MATH] at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with [MATH] public bits.
tldr: The paper derives convex-split bounds using binary quantum hypothesis tests and applies them to one-shot private communication and secret-key distillation.
motivation: The convex-split lemma is a key tool for bounding trace distance in quantum information, but tighter and more operationally transparent proofs are valuable for one-shot cryptographic tasks.
method: It converts measurements on many independent systems plus a reference into binary hypothesis tests on a single system and reference, then averages signal-acceptance probability bounds to control normalized trace distance.
result: The bounds characterize how many independent systems suffice to hide a correlated system, yield one-shot private-communication and one-way secret-key rates with public information, and recover known Gaussian corrections in a finite-alphabet model.
conclusion: Binary quantum hypothesis testing provides a flexible route to convex splitting and gives tight one-shot bounds relevant to quantum cryptography.

A second bound provides a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds are proven for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. The framework is then applied to compare two distributions for the location of the hidden system, yielding one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, the authors recover known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from n independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by log2 n + O(1) at fixed errors. title: Entanglement Geometry Beyond Polygons: Graph-Theoretic Entanglement Inequalities
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement entropies of pure multipartite states can be constrained by organizing subsystem cuts as edges (hyperedges) of graphs (hypergraphs). Starting from the one-party entanglement polygon inequality, we derive these constraints from strong subadditivity and pure-state complementarity, with optimal coefficients and explicit equality conditions. Our central result determines, for a distinguished two-party cut and an arbitrary weighted family of cuts, the optimal polygon coefficient: the smallest total weight of the cuts separating a member of the distinguished pair from a remaining party. A refinement involving three mutual information terms gives the exact minimum of the weighted sum at fixed entropies of the two parties and of their union, attained by at most three independent bipartite pure states. This criterion recovers the cycle and complete-graph inequalities and shows that uniform incidence parity, which we prove sufficient for polygon inequalities on hypergraphs, is not necessary. Averaging strong subadditivity over both sides of a bipartition gives a sharp [MATH]-marginal inequality with coefficient [MATH], and we determine uniformly optimal coefficients for collective hyperstar inequalities. For paths and overlapping hyperchains, the deficits are exact sums of conditional mutual information terms; genuinely multipartite entangled cluster states saturate the hyperchain inequality while the chain inequality remains strict. We characterize pure chain equality states, bound the trace distance to cycle equality states independently of the number of parties and local dimensions, and obtain bond-dimension bounds for matrix product states and sequential-recovery error estimates.
tldr: The paper derives graph- and hypergraph-theoretic entanglement inequalities for pure multipartite states from strong subadditivity and complementarity, with optimal coefficients and equality conditions.
motivation: Entanglement entropy constraints such as polygon inequalities are useful for characterizing multipartite entanglement, but a general graph-theoretic framework with optimal coefficients and sharp equality conditions was lacking.
method: The author formulates subsystem cuts as edges or hyperedges of graphs and hypergraphs, derives inequalities from strong subadditivity and pure-state complementarity, and determines optimal polygon coefficients via weighted cut-separation arguments.
result: The central result gives the optimal coefficient for a distinguished two-party cut and arbitrary weighted cut family, recovers cycle and complete-graph inequalities, proves uniform incidence parity sufficient but not necessary for hypergraph polygon inequalities, and derives sharp marginal, hyperstar, path, and hyperchain inequalities with equality-state and MPS bond-dimension bounds.
conclusion: The work provides a unified graph-theoretic framework for entanglement entropy inequalities beyond simple polygons, with applications to characterizing genuinely multipartite entangled cluster states and bounding matrix product state bond dimensions.

title: Tunable Source Of Entangled Microwaves By Nonlinear Scattering Of Magnons
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a route to prepare entangled states of microwaves propagating in spatially separated transmission lines using the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of ferromagnetic spin waves (magnons). We first show that a driven magnon mode can produce entangled magnon pairs at low temperatures by spontaneous parametric down-conversion enabled by three-magnon processes. The anisotropic magnon properties in thin films result in strict phase-matching conditions which allow only a well-defined pair of magnon modes to be amplified. This mode selectivity allows to out-couple each amplified mode to an independent microwave transmission line, producing non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement with current experimental parameters. In addition, we prove that the frequency difference between the two entangled microwaves can be dynamically tuned across a few-GHz range by changing the orientation of a bias magnetic field. Our figures of merit - .g., the amount of microwave entanglement - can be largely improved by optimizing material and geometry. Our work establishes that quantum states of propagating magnons can be created by their nonlinear dynamics alone, and opens a pathway toward integrating magnons in hybrid quantum platforms.
tldr: The paper proposes a tunable source of entangled propagating microwaves generated by nonlinear magnon dynamics in ferromagnetic thin films.
motivation: Entangled microwave sources are important for hybrid quantum platforms, but generating non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement with tunable frequency remains challenging.
method: A driven magnon mode undergoes spontaneous parametric down-conversion via three-magnon processes, with phase matching selecting a specific magnon pair that is out-coupled to separate microwave transmission lines.
result: The scheme produces non-degenerate entangled microwave beams under current experimental parameters, and the frequency difference can be tuned over a few-GHz range by rotating the bias magnetic field.
conclusion: Nonlinear magnon dynamics alone can create quantum states of propagating magnons and entangled microwaves, opening a route to integrate magnons into hybrid quantum platforms.

title: The Clifford Hierarchy From Clifford Stabilizers In 2d
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Bravyi-K\"onig theorem limits the constant-depth logical gates of 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to be in the Clifford group. Known qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers exceed it by only one level of the Clifford hierarchy, and this was conjectured to hold generally. We show that this bound can be completely bypassed, and that topological codes with Clifford stabilizers in 2D can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. We present two explicit constructions of codes based on copies of the quantum doubles of [MATH] and [MATH], with [MATH] logical qubits and a logical [MATH] gate, which is at level [MATH] of the Clifford hierarchy. The physical circuits realizing the gates consist only of physical [MATH] or [MATH] gates. The main new ingredient comes from the logical encoding, which depends crucially on non-Abelian group multiplication.
tldr: The paper shows that 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes with Clifford stabilizers can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy, bypassing the usual Bravyi-König-type bound.
motivation: Bravyi-König limits constant-depth logical gates in 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to the Clifford group, and existing qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers were conjectured to exceed this by at most one level.
method: The authors construct two explicit families of codes based on copies of quantum doubles of non-Abelian groups, with logical encodings that exploit non-Abelian group multiplication and physical circuits composed only of physical Clifford gates.
result: They obtain codes with logical qubits and a logical gate at an arbitrarily high level of the Clifford hierarchy, demonstrating that the conjectured limitation can be completely evaded in 2D.
conclusion: This work expands the landscape of fault-tolerant logical gates in topological stabilizer codes and highlights non-Abelian encoding structures as a resource for high-level Clifford hierarchy gates.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper challenges the Bravyi-König theorem, which states that constant-depth logical gates in 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes are limited to the Clifford group. The authors demonstrate that this bound can be completely bypassed by constructing 2D topological codes with Clifford stabilizers that realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. They present two explicit constructions based on copies of the quantum doubles of the groups D4 and Z2, each encoding k logical qubits and featuring a logical C^{k-1}Z gate, which lies at level k of the Clifford hierarchy. The physical circuits implementing these gates use only physical Z or CZ gates. The key innovation is a logical encoding that crucially depends on non-Abelian group multiplication, enabling the realization of higher-level Clifford gates without violating the stabilizer formalism. title: Generation Of Coherent-state Schr\"{o}dinger Cat States In A Two-photon Jaynes-Cummings Model Implemented With Josephson Junctions
authors: Hiroo Azuma, William J. Munro, Kae Nemoto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the generation of coherent-state Schr\"{o}dinger cat states using a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) implemented in a Josephson-junction quantum circuit. We consider a specific superconducting flux-qubit implementation and estimate the resulting two-photon coupling constant. We numerically examine three types of noise: magnetic flux noise with [MATH] fluctuations, energy relaxation associated with the flux-qubit [MATH] decay, and photon loss in the bosonic mode obtained by quantizing the phase variable of the dc SQUID used for qubit readout. We find that photon loss has a particularly significant effect on cat-state fidelity. We also investigate the time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis for the [MATH]-photon JCM ([MATH]), starting from a coherent bosonic state. Finally, we assume that the bosonic mode is initially prepared in a displaced thermal state and then decoupled from the heat bath. We study the subsequent unitary evolution to determine how the initial temperature affects the fidelity and Wigner function of the generated cat states.

method: The authors estimate the two-photon coupling for a specific flux-qubit circuit and numerically simulate magnetic flux noise, qubit energy relaxation, and photon loss, also studying Pegg-Barnett phase evolution and displaced thermal initial states.
result: Photon loss is found to be particularly detrimental to cat-state fidelity, and the initial thermal occupation affects both fidelity and the Wigner function of the generated states.
conclusion: The two-photon Jaynes-Cummings platform is promising for cat-state generation, but suppressing photon loss is critical for high-fidelity operation.

title: Remote Use Of Quantum Machines In The Adversarial Scenario
authors: Mir Alimuddin, Leonardo Zambrano, Antonio Ac\'in
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Networked quantum technologies allow users to operate quantum machines hosted by remote servers, but classical commands alone cannot ensure that only the intended user can prepare the useful inputs that activate them. We formulate the problem of adversarial remote use of quantum machines in the framework of quantum resource theories. A device controlled by Bob is correlated to a remote user, Alice, through a bipartite state, and also to an adversary Eve holding its purification. Alice and Eve compete to programme Bob's machine by remotely preparing its inputs: the conditional state carries the quantum resource, while the measurement outcome selects the machine operation. Remote use is truly advantageous when Alice is guaranteed to unlock a larger average task value than the adversary Eve, given the same marginal state of Bob. We show that for tasks with a convex figure of merit, the competition is governed by complementary upper roofs and, for spectral tasks, where the figure of merit is invariant under unitary operations, by a corresponding entanglement imbalance. Purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation show that the same noisy state may secure exclusivity one machine but not another. Finally, we order Alice's and Eve's complete programming powers through a task-independent simulation preorder, based on the ensembles each party can prepare on Bob's side. Shared quantum correlations thereby become a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines.
tldr: The paper formulates adversarial remote use of quantum machines within quantum resource theories and shows when a remote user can outperform an adversary in programming the device.
motivation: Networked quantum technologies require secure access control for remote quantum machines, but classical commands alone cannot guarantee that only the intended user can activate useful inputs.
method: The authors model a Bob-controlled device correlated with remote user Alice and adversary Eve via a bipartite state and its purification, then analyze remote input preparation using convex figures of merit, complementary upper roofs, entanglement imbalance, and a task-independent simulation preorder.
result: For convex tasks, Alice's advantage over Eve is governed by complementary upper roofs; for spectral tasks, by an entanglement imbalance, with examples from purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation showing machine-dependent exclusivity.
conclusion: Shared quantum correlations become a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines, and Alice's and Eve's programming powers can be ordered by a simulation preorder based on preparable ensembles.

title: Modeling Couplings And Quench Dynamics Of Hundred-qubit Quantum Processors
authors: Simon Pettersson Fors, Eric Dj\"aknegren, Jorge Fern\'andez-Pend\'as, Anton Frisk Kockum
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processors now operate beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, yet their design and verification rest on precise models of the device. Understanding which properties of quantum processors can still be predicted on classical computers is central both to building these machines and to delimiting claims of quantum advantage. Here we address this question at the device level, using continuous unitary transformations to derive effective Hamiltonians non-perturbatively for two-dimensional superconducting processors at a cost polynomial in qubit number. For a 96-transmon array with tunable couplers, we extract the effective qubit couplings, state-dependent interactions (e.g., ZZ couplings), and eigenstate locality that guide processor design. This computation parallelizes over tensor contractions and thus takes an hour at most per design point on a single GPU, enabling rapid design iterations of the full array. Combining these effective models with semiclassical sampling, we then predict the quench dynamics of 100 qubits and 180 couplers at half filling, a sector of dimension [MATH], and validate the approach against exact dynamics of smaller arrays. We show that our approach captures relaxation, thermalization, and transport, but not the bitstring statistics underlying cross-entropy benchmarks. The predicted transport carries a fingerprint of the device: under a staggered detuning, excitations cross over from ballistic to diffusive spreading, slow down at a doublon resonance, and diffuse at different rates on each sublattice. Our results chart which observables lie within classical reach and offer a practical tool for designing future devices.
tldr: The paper develops non-perturbative effective Hamiltonian models for large superconducting transmon processors and uses them to predict quench dynamics and transport fingerprints in a 100-qubit array.
motivation: Quantum processors are now beyond exact classical simulation, so understanding which device-level properties remain classically predictable is important for design, verification, and delimiting quantum advantage claims.
method: They apply continuous unitary transformations to derive effective Hamiltonians for 2D superconducting transmon arrays with tunable couplers at polynomial cost, then combine these models with semiclassical sampling to simulate quench dynamics.
result: For a 96-transmon array they extract effective couplings, ZZ interactions, and eigenstate locality; for 100 qubits at half filling they capture relaxation, thermalization, and transport, including ballistic-to-diffusive crossover and doublon-resonance slowing, but not bitstring statistics for cross-entropy benchmarks.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical GPU-efficient tool for designing superconducting processors and clarifies which observables are classically accessible, while also identifying limits for benchmarking quantum advantage.

title: A Measurement-free Quantum Error Correction Protocol For Superconducting Cavities
authors: Q. Rumman Rahman, S. M. Girvin, D. K. Weiss
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock [MATH] encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
tldr: The paper proposes and numerically demonstrates a measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting microwave cavities that corrects single-photon loss with 99% fidelity and achieves break-even logical lifetime.
motivation: Large-scale quantum computation requires quantum error correction, and correcting dominant physical errors at a lower level can reduce the demands placed on an outer code.
method: The authors adapt a coherent-control, measurement-free QEC scheme to a circuit QED architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction nonlinear elements, encoding a logical qubit in a lowest-order binomial code in one cavity with two ancilla cavities.
result: Using experimentally realistic parameters, the protocol corrects single-photon loss with 99% fidelity and extends the logical lifetime by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock encoding, surpassing break-even performance.
conclusion: The work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC in superconducting cavity architectures for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Passive Memories Beyond The Ising Model: From Sfq To Gkp
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-correcting quantum memories are spin Hamiltonians that aim to generalize the classical memory of the magnetic hard disk (i.e. ferromagnetic Ising model) to protect against both bit flips and phase flips. Beyond the magnetic hard disk, there are other passive classical memories that are used in modern computers, notably: the flash memory in laptops (which traps charge on a conducting island), and the flux storage loop in single-flux quantum (SFQ) logic (which traps flux in a superconducting loop). In this paper we review how storage and writing work in these two classical memories, drawing analogies to the charge qubit and the flux qubit. Protection in these systems derives not from scaling a lattice to the thermodynamic limit, but from a large, tunable energy barrier that separates codewords during memory, yet can be suppressed during a write. Towards protecting a qubit: We introduce a 2D ``floating XY model'' that combines the exponential (phase-flip) protection of the floating charge island with the polynomial (bit-flip) protection of the ferromagnetic XY model. We also study a self-dual superconducting circuit that hosts GKP codewords as symmetry-broken ground states of a [MATH]-symmetric circuit, and discuss its protection and limitations.

method: It draws analogies between flash/SFQ classical memories and charge/flux qubits, introduces a 2D floating XY model, and analyzes a self-dual superconducting circuit whose symmetry-broken ground states are GKP codewords.
result: The floating XY model combines exponential phase-flip protection with polynomial bit-flip protection, while the self-dual circuit realizes GKP codewords with discussed protection and limitations.
conclusion: Passive quantum memory designs may exploit large tunable energy barriers and superconducting-circuit analogies, though practical protection constraints remain.

title: Generalizing And Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration For Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs. We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at [URL] and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at [URL].

title: Resilience Of Emergent Hamiltonian Quantum Memories In The Presence Of Noise
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emergent Hamiltonians can freeze an entangled state prepared through coherent evolution, since that state is an eigenstate of the Hamiltonian under which it is then stored. For a product of Bell pairs prepared from a density wave in an engineered chain, a selection rule prevents local density noise from connecting the target to any of its degenerate partners, so that rescaling the storage Hamiltonian by a factor [MATH] moves every transition this noise drives. Under [MATH] noise, the storage time then grows in proportion to [MATH], a result we confirm by evolving the memory under explicit classical [MATH] fields, whereas for an Ohmic bath the most favorable scale depends on its cutoff. Fermionic loss, treated as a solvable model, includes a transition that rescaling leaves at zero frequency, and an energy shift [MATH] per particle moves it away from zero, with an exact orbital solution giving the resulting lifetimes. Finally, among number-conserving quadratic reference Hamiltonians, [MATH] and [MATH] are the only controls that keep the storage Hamiltonian nearest neighbor at every time along the preparation, so that the protocol combines local freezing with control over the storage spectrum.

title: Birthday-Scale Non-Adaptive Security For Strong Pseudorandom Unitaries

abstract: ArXiv:2611.25038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) are efficiently implementable unitary ensembles that are computationally indistinguishable from Haar-random unitaries, providing efficient substitutes for Haar-randomness in quantum information and cryptography. In this work, we prove birthday-scale non-adaptive security for the DPFC (Clifford-Phase-Permutation-Clifford) strong PRU candidate. For an [MATH]-dimensional unitary, allowing arbitrary entangled inputs and coherent superpositions of query types, we show that DPFC can withstand [MATH] queries. This matches the best known query complexity even for PRUs that are not strong, compared with [MATH] for [MATH] in previous strong-PRU analyses. Our proof utilizes two techniques from previous works: the EPR-sector decomposition of Schuster et al. (arXiv 2025), previously used for unitary designs but not for PRUs, and the path-recording framework of Ma and Huang (STOC 2025), previously used for adaptive security analysis. We complement the non-adaptive security result with an upper bound in the adaptive setting, showing that DPFC cannot remain secure for [MATH] queries.

title: Interfacing Silicon Nitride Nanophotonics With Cuprous Oxide Rydberg Excitons
authors: Artem Kryvobok, Hamza Ather, Julio Herreros Garc\'ia, Ziqi Niu, Abhishek Bharatbhai Solanki, Vahagn Mkhitaryan, Benjamin Cerjan, Alexandra Boltasseva, Vladimir M. Shalaev, Hadiseh Alaeian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg excitons in cuprous oxide (Cu[MATH]O), the solid-state counterpart of Rydberg atoms, are hydrogen-like electron--hole quasi-particles with micron-sized wavefunctions and strong long-range interactions that promise optical nonlinearities at the few-photon level. Exploiting them in a waveguide quantum electrodynamics (WQED) setting can enable what atomic Rydberg platforms achieve only with ultrahigh vacuum and laser cooling/trapping---a guided optical mode interfaced with the Rydberg medium---while adding the scalability and advanced fabrication of integrated photonics. Here we demonstrate a monolithic, CMOS-compatible interface of Cu[MATH]O Rydberg excitons with a SiN[MATH] nanophotonic waveguide. Under non-resonant excitation, excitonic emission from the Cu[MATH]O microcrystal is coupled to the guided mode, routed along the waveguide, and collected from an output grating. The spectrum shows the phonon-assisted 1[MATH] orthoexciton emission together with the low-lying 2[MATH] and 3[MATH] lines of the yellow Rydberg series. title: Characterizing A Neutral Atom Quantum Simulator Accessible In Cloud
authors: Andrea Muratori, Francesco Minardi, Tommaso Calarco, Felix Motzoi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulators have become a reality in recent years, with several platforms now remotely accessible through the cloud. These systems give researchers the opportunity to run quantum programs without requiring either a dedicated laboratory or extensive experimental expertise, and, in several cases, they have already enabled the execution of relevant protocols with remarkable results. However, despite the impressive progress in the performance of these machines, they still suffer from various noise sources, some of which are not always completely clear to the end user, which limits their applicability to tasks that are sufficiently robust against noise of various kinds. In this work, we investigate the behavior of Fresnel, a remotely accessible neutral-atom analog quantum simulator provided by Pasqal. We design and perform a series of experiments probing the machine's response to various pulse sequences and experimental settings, and identify the main noise sources affecting its dynamics. Based on these data, we construct an effective model of the system's noisy evolution and use numerical optimization to infer the noise strengths. The resulting model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics, showing how effective noise models can be built for cloud-based quantum resources.

method: The authors design and run pulse-sequence experiments on the Fresnel neutral-atom simulator, probe its response to different settings, identify dominant noise sources, and use numerical optimization to fit an effective noisy-evolution model.
result: The inferred effective model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics and quantifies the main noise strengths affecting the device.
conclusion: Effective noise models can be constructed for cloud-accessible quantum resources, improving their usability and enabling more robust protocol design on neutral-atom simulators.

title: Optimal Impure $(r,\delta)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes With Explicit Minimum Localities
authors: Yang Li, Shitao Li, Gaojun Luo, San Ling
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes with [MATH]-locality ([MATH]-qLRCs) are quantum error-correcting codes in which [MATH] erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only [MATH] other qudits. The minimum locality of a qLRC is the least [MATH] such that it has [MATH]-locality. This paper aims to construct optimal impure [MATH]-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets and explicit minimum localities, where the optimality is measured by the Singleton-like bound of Guruswami, Kshirsagar, and Trivedi (GKT-optimal). Such qLRCs have particular advantages in recovering as many quantum erasures as possible while operating in parallel and with minimal qudit access overhead. We first characterize the recovering sets and the minimum locality of any CSS code by local relative distances, which are relative minimum distances of punctured codes with respect to shortened codes. We then construct impure qLRCs as CSS codes from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes. Grouping the monomials by their degree in the last variable, we reduce both their minimum distances and their local recovery to nested pairs of codes in the remaining variables, and the coordinates with the same values of these variables form disjoint recovering sets. In this way, we obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure [MATH]-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets, and determine their minimum localities and the recovering sets attaining them for every admissible [MATH], except for a partial range of [MATH] in one family. These minimum localities need not be monotone in [MATH]. In particular, two of the families contain GKT-optimal impure subfamilies of CSS codes CSS[MATH] with [MATH]-locality for some [MATH], where [MATH] is the length of [MATH].

method: The authors characterize recovering sets and minimum locality of CSS codes via local relative distances, then build impure qLRCs from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes and group monomials by degree to obtain disjoint recovering sets.
result: They obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets and determine their minimum localities and recovering sets for almost all admissible parameters, noting that minimum locality need not be monotone.
conclusion: The work provides explicit optimal impure quantum locally recoverable code families with controlled locality, advancing coding-theoretic constructions relevant to quantum error correction.

title: Counterfactual Attribution Of Surface-code Failures Under non-Pauli Noise: Dependence On Trajectory Pairing
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under Pauli noise in a stabilizer memory, attributing a quantum error-correction failure to the noise that caused it has a canonical answer; under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals. We define a failing shot's cause set, the sites whose removal alone removes the failure, and separate it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing enters wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making it maximal at every random step selects shared random numbers, while continuity does not. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites, against 2.3% under the twirl. Other admissible pairings move the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 to 80 times the minimum the marginals allow, yet pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models. Shot-level attributions should therefore state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside.
tldr: The paper analyzes how counterfactual attribution of surface-code failures under non-Pauli noise depends on trajectory pairing, distinguishing pairing-dependent cause sets from pairing-independent effects.
motivation: Error-correction failure attribution is well-defined for Pauli noise but ambiguous under non-Pauli noise, where trajectory pairing with counterfactuals affects shot-level causal claims.
method: The authors define cause sets as sites whose removal alone eliminates a failure and compare exact non-Pauli noise with its Pauli twirl in a distance-three surface code under different admissible trajectory pairings.
result: Although exact noise and its twirl fail at equivalent rates within a registered margin, shared random draws yield 20.2% of exact-noise failures requiring three or more sites versus 2.3% under the twirl; other pairings vary mean coherent cause count by up to 80 times the marginal minimum.
conclusion: Shot-level attributions should explicitly report trajectory pairing and also present pairing-independent quantities, since pairing-independent metrics barely separate exact non-Pauli noise from its Pauli twirl.

Under Pauli noise, the canonical cause of a failure is the set of faults that, if removed, would have prevented the failure. For non-Pauli noise, the authors show that this attribution is not unique: it depends on how noise trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals (i.e., how random draws are coupled). They introduce the concept of a 'cause set' for a failing shot—the sites whose removal alone removes the failure—and distinguish it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing becomes relevant when a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making the pairing maximal at every random step corresponds to shared random numbers, while continuity does not require such maximal pairing. title: Syndrome-based Calibration Using Gate-Error Amplification
authors: Andrew T. Kamen, Arielle Sanford, Frederic T. Chong, Andy J. Goldschmidt, Siddharth Dangwal
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Gate-Error Amplification for Recalibration with Syndromes (GEARS), a runtime calibration framework that uses gate-error amplification to efficiently tune control parameters during quantum error correction. Maintaining reliable control of large qubit arrays throughout hours-long computations requires repeated calibration to compensate for hardware drift. In conventional calibration, targeted qubits are temporarily removed from the code, introducing non-negligible space-time overhead. An elegant alternative uses syndrome information already collected during error correction as feedback for in situ recalibration, but acquiring signal requires sufficient (1) measurement budget or (2) probe strength, i.e., the size of deliberate control perturbations. More measurements improve statistical precision but result in slower control updates, while stronger perturbations produce larger calibration signals at the cost of additional errors. GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with an established gate characterization technique called gate-error amplification. Our approach repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing. Surface code simulations show that GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by approximately a factor of eight at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces excess expected logical failures by approximately 31-40% relative to calibration without amplification across the evaluated execution windows. Under time-dependent drift, GEARS increases the estimated critical drift frequency by approximately 1.9x. These results indicate that deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.
tldr: GEARS is a runtime calibration framework that amplifies gate errors in repeated CZ gates to strengthen syndrome-based feedback signals, reducing the measurement budget needed to track hardware drift during surface-code quantum error correction.
motivation: Hours-long fault-tolerant computations require repeated recalibration to counter drift, but conventional calibration removes qubits from the code (space-time overhead) while purely syndrome-based in-situ calibration is limited by the trade-off between measurement budget and probe strength.
method: The authors augment syndrome-based calibration with gate-error amplification, repeating selected CZ gates and probing their controls in spatially separated groups to boost local signal while limiting logical cost; they evaluate this in surface-code simulations with closed-loop calibration under static and time-dependent drift.
result: Depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by roughly 8x at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength, cuts excess expected logical failures by 31-40% in closed-loop operation, and increases the estimated critical drift frequency by about 1.9x.
conclusion: Deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation is a viable way to improve long-time performance of quantum computations, though the benefit is an engineering/control-level improvement rather than a new information-theoretic result.

title: Compiling Constraints Into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. A compiler turns constraints into this wiring with a number of auxiliary clauses that grows only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints. Restricting the search to feasible states reduces constraint handling to move design, and we show that the fastest-annealing moves are not those that mix fastest but those that lower the deepest energy barriers, and that moves chosen from the objective lower them further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on a field-programmable gate array, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 [MATH]s per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.
tldr: The paper presents a compiler for higher-order neuromorphic Ising machines that enforces constraints via programmable feasible-state moves rather than energy penalties, with an application to surface-code decoding.
motivation: Practical combinatorial optimization and Ising machines usually handle constraints through penalty terms, which create high barriers between feasible solutions and slow down annealing.
method: The authors design an autoencoder-like higher-order Ising machine in which inner-layer neurons represent multi-spin moves and outer-layer neurons switch move-energy connections; a compiler translates parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition, and permutation constraints into polynomial-size wiring.
result: The machine requires far fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines on third-order graph matching, and an FPGA implementation decodes surface codes with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to distance 15 and real-time decoding up to distance 9 under noisy syndrome measurements.
conclusion: Compiling constraints into feasible-state moves can improve Ising-machine optimization and provides a practical hardware decoder for quantum error-correcting surface codes.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine that enforces constraints in combinatorial optimization through programmable multi-spin transitions rather than energy penalties. The architecture is autoencoder-like: inner-layer neurons represent moves (families of multi-spin flips that map feasible states to feasible states), outer-layer neurons multiplicatively gate the energy-change signals and state updates via connections. A compiler translates constraints into this wiring, with auxiliary clauses growing only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition, and permutation constraints. By restricting the search to feasible states, constraint handling reduces to move design. The authors show that the fastest-annealing moves are those that lower the deepest energy barriers, not those that mix fastest, and that moves chosen from the objective lower barriers further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine requires orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on an FPGA, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to distance 15 within 52 μs per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.
key_contributions: A higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine architecture that enforces constraints via programmable multi-spin transitions (moves) instead of energy penalties, using an autoencoder-like network with multiplicative gating.
A compiler that maps constraints (parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition, permutation) into the machine's wiring with polynomial auxiliary clause growth.
Demonstration that move design governs annealing speed: moves lowering the deepest energy barriers outperform those with fast mixing, and objective-informed moves outperform random ones.
Empirical results on third-order graph matching showing orders-of-magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines.

FPGA implementation as a surface code sampler achieving maximum-likelihood accuracy up to distance 15 in 52 μs per shot and real-time decoding for distance 9 under noisy syndrome measurements, with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The core methodological innovation is the replacement of penalty terms with constraint-preserving moves. The machine's state space is restricted to feasible configurations, and each inner-layer neuron encodes a move—a multi-spin transition that maps any feasible state to another feasible state. Outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on/off the connections that transmit energy changes and state updates, effectively implementing a higher-order interaction. A compiler translates constraints into this wiring; for common constraint types, the number of auxiliary clauses grows polynomially, avoiding the exponential blow-up typical of penalty-based encodings. The authors analyze annealing dynamics by relating move selection to energy barrier lowering, showing that the deepest barriers dominate annealing time. They test the approach on third-order graph matching and on surface code decoding, implementing the latter on an FPGA as a sampler. The surface code decoding uses the machine to sample from a distribution corresponding to the maximum-likelihood decoder, leveraging the constraint-preserving moves to handle the syndrome constraints efficiently.
deep_read.results_analysis: On third-order graph matching, the machine requires orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines, demonstrating the efficiency of constraint-preserving moves. For surface code decoding, the FPGA implementation achieves maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 μs per shot. Under noisy syndrome measurements, it decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9, with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders. These results indicate that the higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can serve as a fast and accurate decoder for quantum error correction, potentially enabling real-time decoding in fault-tolerant quantum computing. title: High-Dimensional Structured Light Tomography With A Tilted Lens
authors: Altilano C. Barbosa, Isaac Tribaldo, Amanda K. Fritsch, Marcos G. de Oliveira, Gabriel Molina-Terriza, Antonio Z. Khoury
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate high-dimensional spatial mode tomography using intensity measurements and the astigmatic transformation implemented with a tilted lens. We improve the method previously published in Ref. [1] to perform the spatial tomography not restricted to a fixed order, which allowed us to achieve good fidelity for a mode space dimension as high as [MATH]. Since the literature is not unanimous, we also present a comprehensive revision of light propagation through a tilted lens for an accurate description of the transformation used for tomography. We derive its effective focal lengths, and analyze its role as an astigmatic mode converter. Moreover, we establish its explicit domain of validity within the Hermite-Gaussian basis.
tldr: The paper develops high-dimensional spatial-mode tomography using a tilted lens and characterizes the astigmatic transformation in the Hermite-Gaussian basis.
motivation: Spatial-mode tomography is needed for characterizing high-dimensional optical states, but existing tilted-lens methods are restricted to fixed mode order and lack a consistent propagation description.
method: Uses intensity measurements after an astigmatic transformation from a tilted lens, derives effective focal lengths and validity domain, and extends reconstruction beyond fixed order.
result: Achieves good fidelity for high-dimensional mode spaces and provides a comprehensive revision of tilted-lens propagation as an astigmatic mode converter.
conclusion: The improved tomography method is useful for structured-light characterization, though its direct quantum-information-theoretic impact is limited.

title: The Computational Complexity Of Bosonic Lindbladian Fixed Points
authors: En-Jui Kuo, Arsalan Motamedi, Mohammad Hafezi, Saeed Mehraban
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states, or fixed points, of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions. While the complexity of transient bosonic dynamics has been investigated, understanding the computational power of bosonic fixed points requires addressing subtleties of infinite-dimensional systems, including the existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states. We establish a broad complexity landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. First, we show that universal quantum computation can be embedded into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a bosonic Lindbladian with a Hamiltonian of degree at most twelve and only linear photon loss. Moreover, this fixed point can be prepared from vacuum in polynomial time. On the classical side, we identify Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping that admit efficient photon-number sampling and establish stability of classical approximability under sufficiently weak non-Gaussian Kerr perturbations. Conversely, for Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping, we establish hardness of exact sampling under constant-rate linear loss and hardness of approximate sampling at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures. We also relate sampling from non-Gaussian fixed points to variants of boson sampling. Finally, we prove that deciding the existence of a stationary density operator is [MATH]-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators acting on at most four modes.
tldr: The paper maps the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from fixed points of bosonic Lindbladians, spanning universal quantum computation, classical simulability, sampling hardness, and undecidability.
motivation: Transient bosonic dynamics have been studied, but fixed points involve subtleties of infinite-dimensional open quantum systems, including existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states.
method: The authors analyze bounded-degree polynomial bosonic Lindbladians and establish complexity-theoretic reductions and hardness results for observable estimation and stationary-state sampling, including Gaussian and non-Gaussian regimes.
result: They embed universal quantum computation into fixed-point observable estimation, identify efficiently simulable Gaussian regimes, prove sampling hardness under boson-sampling conjectures, and show that deciding existence of a stationary density operator is hard even for purely dissipative low-degree Lindbladians.
conclusion: Bosonic Lindbladian fixed points exhibit a rich complexity landscape, ranging from universal quantum computational power to classical simulability and undecidability, with implications for open quantum systems and quantum complexity theory.

title: A Basis-Dependent Kernel For Learning Quantum Phases Of Matter
authors: Clemens Lindner, Vin\'icius Mohr, Adri\'an P\'erez-Salinas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying the phases of a quantum many-body system as its parameters vary is a central problem in condensed-matter physics. Data-driven approaches address this task by comparing quantum states, for instance through their fidelity, and locating transitions where these comparisons change abruptly. In this work, we introduce the inverse participation ratio (IPR) kernel, a kernel method built for learning quantum phases of matter from IPRs in physically motivated bases. Unlike fidelity-based kernels, the IPR kernel can identify states with physically meaningful similarity even when they are orthogonal. We test the method on ground states of the transverse-field Ising (TFIM) and Heisenberg XXZ models. For TFIM Gibbs states, we further show that the IPR kernel retains phase-relevant structure over a range of nonzero temperatures where the phase signal of fidelity-based kernels is already degraded. More broadly, our results suggest that quantum kernels benefit more from feature maps tailored to the physics of the problem than from maximal expressivity.
tldr: The paper introduces an inverse participation ratio (IPR) kernel for learning quantum phases of matter from physically motivated bases, showing advantages over fidelity-based kernels especially for orthogonal states and finite-temperature Gibbs states.
motivation: Identifying quantum many-body phases as parameters vary is central in condensed-matter physics, and data-driven methods often rely on fidelity comparisons that fail for orthogonal states or degrade at nonzero temperature.
method: The authors define a kernel based on inverse participation ratios in chosen physical bases and test it on ground states of the transverse-field Ising and Heisenberg XXZ models, also studying TFIM Gibbs states at nonzero temperature.
result: The IPR kernel identifies physically meaningful similarity even for orthogonal states and retains phase-relevant structure over a temperature range where fidelity-based kernels lose phase signal.
conclusion: Quantum kernels benefit more from feature maps tailored to the physics of the problem than from maximal expressivity, suggesting physics-informed kernel design for learning quantum phases.

title: Certified Discovery Of Quantum Phase Diagrams
authors: Yuanxi Liu, John Preskill, Hsin-Yuan Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a machine provably discover new quantum phases of matter? We show that the answer is yes under physically motivated assumptions. For any smooth family of geometrically local Hamiltonians, we construct an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs the phase diagram to prescribed accuracy and provides a verifiable certificate for every transition it reports. The algorithm takes as input only a classical description of the family together with unverified preparations of reference ground states; no order parameter, symmetry-breaking pattern, or training data are supplied. It succeeds provided that at least one preparation is correct in each gapped region of parameter space. The algorithm explores parameter space by quasi-adiabatically or adiabatically transporting each reference state, detecting the approach of a phase boundary by tapping the transported state with a frequency-filtered local probe: excitations created by the probe witness the closing of the energy gap. We prove that the gap closing for continuous phase transitions can always be detected using the frequency-filtered gradient of the Hamiltonian. The gap-detecting measurement is gentle, so when the ground state is unique a single reusable copy of each reference ground state supports the full exploration (for degenerate ground states, polynomially many copies suffice). The quantum algorithm runs in polynomial time at inverse-polynomial gap resolution. We also give a classical algorithm that runs in quasipolynomial time at constant gap resolution. Numerical experiments demonstrate how our algorithm accurately determines the phase structure of several model quantum systems.
tldr: The authors give an efficient quantum algorithm that provably outputs the phase diagram of a smooth family of geometrically local Hamiltonians, with verifiable certificates for each reported phase transition, using only classical descriptions and unverified reference ground states.
motivation: Discovering new quantum phases of matter typically requires order parameters, symmetries, or training data, and there is no guarantee that machine-learned phase boundaries are correct. The authors ask whether a machine can provably and certifiably discover phase diagrams under physically motivated assumptions.
method: Each reference ground state is transported quasi-adiabatically through parameter space, and approaching a phase boundary is detected by a frequency-filtered local probe whose excitations witness gap closing; the gentle nature of the measurement allows a single reusable copy per gapped region, and a quasipolynomial-time classical analogue is also provided.
result: The algorithm runs in polynomial time at inverse-polynomial gap resolution, is proven to detect gap closing for continuous phase transitions via the frequency-filtered gradient of the Hamiltonian, and numerical experiments on model systems reproduce known phase structures accurately.
conclusion: Certified, assumption-light discovery of quantum phase diagrams is possible, blending rigorous quantum-algorithm guarantees with practical numerical demonstrations, though the work sits closer to quantum learning theory and condensed-matter phase classification than to information-theoretic or thermodynamic questions.

title: Structure And Complexity Of Perfect Functional Representations
authors: Serhat Emre Coban, Yanina Y. Shkel, Emre Telatar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For given random variables [MATH], functional representation lemma states that there exists a random variable [MATH] and a deterministic function [MATH] such that [MATH], and [MATH] is independent of [MATH]. In other words, [MATH] captures all the information about [MATH] not contained in [MATH]. We refer to [MATH] as a `perfect functional representation' if it satisfies [MATH]. We show that the existence of perfect representation depends solely on the conditional distribution [MATH] and define the corresponding conditional distributions as perfectly representable. We provide a necessary and sufficient condition for [MATH] to be perfectly representable. Moreover, we cast the problem of checking perfect representability as a linear program, give an algorithm whose complexity is polynomial in [MATH] and exponential in [MATH], and prove that deciding perfect representability is NP-complete for rational input matrices encoded in binary.
tldr: The paper studies when a conditional distribution admits a perfect functional representation and characterizes the computational complexity of deciding this property.
motivation: The functional representation lemma is a basic tool in information theory, but conditions for a perfect representation and the complexity of checking them were not fully understood.
method: The authors characterize perfect representability in terms of the conditional distribution, derive necessary and sufficient conditions, formulate the check as a linear program, and analyze its algorithmic and complexity-theoretic properties.
result: They give an algorithm polynomial in one parameter and exponential in another, and prove that deciding perfect representability is NP-complete for rational input matrices encoded in binary.
conclusion: Perfect functional representability is a nontrivial structural and computational property of conditional distributions, with tractable cases but generally NP-complete decision complexity.

title: Correctable Enrollment And One-Transaction Seed Proofs For Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
authors: Xin Jin, Maximillian Liao, Handong Chen, Yi Nancy Li, Junyu Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.
tldr: The paper designs and implements a migration scheme for Ethereum that lets account owners enroll post-quantum keys using existing ECDSA signatures before retirement, with seed-based zero-knowledge proofs serving as a correction/recovery path.
motivation: Shor's algorithm threatens every Ethereum account with a published public key, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH; since the first quantum computer capable of this may remain secret, migration cannot wait for observable thefts and legacy signatures become useless for authentication once keys are extractable.
method: The authors specify rules for cheap pre-retirement PQ key enrollment, a three-layer recursive hash-based STARK seed proof (binding new key, nonce, and fee cap) as a deadline-bounded correction mechanism, and validator switching to hash-based keys at a finalized checkpoint; they prove account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement them in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client.
result: Seed proofs are ~190 KB and fit in one transaction, verify in 38 ms with median 111 s generation on a laptop, and four proofs aggregate; simulations show the 4.45 million accounts with ≥0.1 ETH would take 29.4 days to migrate if all enroll beforehand and 235 days in post-retirement batches of four, with median 19.1-minute mempool delays during mass enrollment exceeding fast-attack key-extraction estimates.
conclusion: The design provides a practical, formally checked path to post-quantum Ethereum, but the mempool latency result implies that owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate via seed proof rather than waiting for enrollment.

title: Accelerating Diffusion Maps On A Quantum Computer: Spectral Filtering And Galerkin Pde Solvers
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion maps generalize principal component analysis (PCA) to nonlinear manifolds, enabling spectral dimensionality reduction, geometric data analysis, and elliptic PDE approximation on point clouds. For large datasets of size [MATH], however, classical matrix operations incur prohibitive [MATH] scaling, even when extracting low-dimensional spectral features or targeted scalar observables. We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework that bypasses explicit graph-Laplacian assembly by exploiting the symmetric factorization [MATH] directly at the block-encoding level. Combining Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), we implement spectral filters of [MATH] to estimate heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, and energy responses, as well as to prepare spectral Galerkin solution states. A common-state construction further allows the block-encoding queries to be used across multiple scalar observables. Under polylogarithmic-cost block-encoding access to [MATH] and state-preparation oracles, our heat-overlap algorithm achieves [MATH] gate complexity at fixed normalized precision, confidence, and spectral scale. Ideal statevector simulations validate our discrete circuit constructions, while a matched approximate-counting benchmark demonstrates the quadratic precision advantage of coherent amplitude estimation for energy readout.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantum algorithmic framework using block encodings, LCU, and QSVT to accelerate diffusion maps for spectral filtering and Galerkin PDE solutions.
motivation: Diffusion maps are powerful for nonlinear dimensionality reduction and PDE approximation, but classical graph-Laplacian operations scale prohibitively with dataset size.
method: The authors avoid explicit graph-Laplacian assembly by block-encoding a symmetric factorization, combining Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted LCU, and QSVT to implement spectral filters and prepare Galerkin solution states.
result: Under polylogarithmic-cost oracle access, the heat-overlap algorithm achieves polylogarithmic gate complexity at fixed precision, with coherent amplitude estimation providing a quadratic precision advantage for energy readout.
conclusion: Quantum algorithms can in principle accelerate diffusion-map-based spectral tasks and PDE solvers, though practical relevance depends on efficient oracle access and fault-tolerant implementation.

title: Atlas: Accelerating Quantum Ftqc Compilation With Optimized Algebraic Rotation Synthesis
authors: Anbang Wu, Pu Pang, Wei Geng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As fault-tolerant quantum computing emerges, Clifford+T gate basis becomes a popular choice where we need to decompose single-qubit rotation gates into gates in this gate basis. Quantum rotation synthesis may lead to remarkable overhead in quantum circuit compilation. Considering variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) applications as an example, a conventional UCCSD ansatz in quantum chemistry can generate [MATH] rotations for [MATH] qubits. Each optimization iteration updates the rotation angles, making rotation synthesis a recurring cost that can delay the VQE training loop. We identify two sources of delay in rotation synthesis: redundant computation during synthesis and uneven synthesis times that leave workers waiting for slow requests. Atlas addresses these costs with three optimizations: search pruning skips invalid synthesis candidates through statistical inference; adaptive arithmetic avoid unnecessary high-overhead big integer/float arithmetic when decomposing the target rotation gate; batch scheduling fills the gap between the synthesis time of varied rotations. Across various benchmarks, synthesis method, and compilation machines, Atlas can consistently accelerate the rotation synthesis process by up to 12.65x.
tldr: Atlas accelerates Clifford+T rotation synthesis for fault-tolerant quantum compilation using search pruning, adaptive arithmetic, and batch scheduling, achieving up to 12.65x speedup.
motivation: As fault-tolerant quantum computing emerges, decomposing single-qubit rotations into Clifford+T gates becomes a recurring bottleneck in compilation, especially for variational algorithms like VQE where angles change each iteration.
method: Atlas identifies two delay sources—redundant computation and uneven synthesis times—and addresses them with three optimizations: statistical search pruning, adaptive precision arithmetic, and batch scheduling to balance worker loads.
result: Across various benchmarks, synthesis methods, and machines, Atlas consistently accelerates rotation synthesis by up to 12.65x compared to baseline methods.
conclusion: The proposed optimizations significantly reduce compilation overhead for fault-tolerant quantum circuits, enabling faster VQE training loops and more efficient quantum algorithm development.

title: From Fips To Fpga With Llm Agents: Measuring What Tests And Reviews Miss In Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
authors: Jungmin Park, Eunha Kim, Wooseop Kim, Seongjoon Cho, Byungho Cha
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.
tldr: An LLM-agent-driven RTL verification workflow is used to port an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 post-quantum accelerator to an FPGA key-custody card, with mutation-based auditing revealing that passing tests overstate verification strength.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly generate both hardware designs and the tests/reviews that validate them, so self-generated evidence is untrustworthy; the authors want an independent, mutation- and formal-check-based audit of such agentic flows.
method: A seven-stage verification-gated workflow is applied to a post-quantum cryptography design port, then audited using tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks, including pre-registered single-model LLM review replays at whole-design and module scope.
result: The port is byte-exact and passes 85 of 285 NIST ACVP interface cases plus 484 ML-DSA known answers, but simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 netlist mutants; scoped review catches known flaws in 54/54 sessions yet planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20, while formal checks flag all of them.
conclusion: Trustworthy agentic hardware verification requires author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.

title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times In Quantum Phase Estimation
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.
tldr: The paper introduces an optimization loop that learns Hamiltonian evolution times in quantum phase estimation to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured phase distributions and improve minimum-eigenvalue accuracy.
motivation: Standard quantum phase estimation suffers from digitization error in estimating phases, limiting eigenvalue accuracy independent of the number of phase qubits.
method: The authors add a parameter-learning optimization loop around a QPE circuit, tuning integer winding evolution times to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalue phases, and test it numerically on quantum magnet models.
result: Minimizing phase-distribution Shannon entropy corresponds to improved analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue, allowing shorter-depth QPE circuits to achieve better accuracy.
conclusion: The approach makes near-term QPE more practical for fundamental science applications, but it is an algorithm-level numerical study outside the user's core quantum information and thermodynamics interests.
