motivation: AI agents increasingly transact with stablecoins, but wallet signatures may not enforce the full commerce mandate specified by the protocol, creating a mismatch between signed authorization and intended payment terms.
method: The authors define nine constraint classes, derive them across 12 authorization configurations including Coinbase's Commerce Payments Protocol, run 31,800 trials on deployed contract code, and test a minimal recipient-contract implementation called MandateLock.
result: All trials match the derivation; committing terms in the signed nonce binds the order, but binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Among sampled USD Coin authorizations on Base, 98.7% followed a path redeemable by any signature holder, while MandateLock rejects all 10,800 modified mandates at 25% higher gas than a recipient-only transfer.
conclusion: The work shows that current crypto payment authorization can leave commerce mandates unbound and demonstrates sufficient conditions and a practical recipient-contract design for enforcing signed AI-agent payment mandates.

title: The Complete Set Of Solutions For The Equations Of Temporal Coupled Mode Theory
authors: Matthew Beutel, Ming Zhou, Shanhui Fan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal coupled mode theory (TCMT) provides a compact description of resonant transport in optical systems in terms of a small set of physically transparent parameters, including the resonant coupling coefficients and direct background scattering matrix. In the formalism of TCMT, the background scattering matrix and the coupling vectors are constrained by time reversal symmetry, reciprocity, and energy conservation. While these constraints are well established, the general so- lution under these is only known for a few cases, in which spatial symmetry simplifies the problem. In this paper, we derive the complete set of solutions for the equations of temporal coupled mode theory that describes lossless single-mode or multi-mode resonators coupled to an arbitrary num- ber of ports. Our derivation utilizes an explicit Takagi decomposition of the symmetric unitary background scattering matrix. We provide a comparison with numerical simulations for both the single and multimode cases.
tldr: The paper derives the complete general solution set of temporal coupled mode theory (TCMT) equations for lossless single- and multi-mode resonators coupled to an arbitrary number of ports.
motivation: TCMT constrains the background scattering matrix and coupling vectors via time-reversal symmetry, reciprocity, and energy conservation, but the full general solution was previously known only for special cases where spatial symmetry simplifies the problem.
method: The authors exploit an explicit Takagi decomposition of the symmetric unitary background scattering matrix to solve the constraint equations in full generality, and validate against numerical simulations for single- and multi-mode cases.
result: A complete parametrization of all allowed coupling vectors and background scattering matrices is obtained for arbitrary port number and mode count, generalizing prior symmetry-restricted solutions.
conclusion: The results provide a general foundational toolkit for constructing physically consistent TCMT models of resonant optical structures, with direct relevance to classical photonic device design rather than quantum information processing.

title: On The Reliability Of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency And Reference-Target Identity
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.
tldr: The paper audits the CyberGym vulnerability-reproduction benchmark, finding task-material inconsistencies and non-target PoC passes that lower effective pass rates.
motivation: CyberGym's evaluation assumes consistent task materials and that a differential crash demonstrates reproduction of the intended vulnerability; the authors test whether these assumptions hold.
method: They perform a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of final PoCs from a complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run using execution checks, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review.
result: They label 338 tasks (22.4%) as materially inconsistent and find 89 non-target plus 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts among 1,286 differential passes, reducing the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%.
conclusion: The findings motivate separate consistency and identity checks when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores, though the identity verdicts need independent validation.

title: On H\"older Equicontinuity Of The Integrated Density Of States For Random Schr\"odinger Operators On $\mathbb{Z}^d$
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a random Schr\"odinger operator [MATH] on [MATH] consisting of a translation invariant hopping matrix [MATH] and a random potential [MATH], given by independently distributed single site potentials with absolutely continuous distributions. Assuming a regularity assumption for the hopping matrix [MATH], we show H\"older continuity of the integrated density of states of [MATH] up to exponents [MATH], independently of the disorder strength [MATH].
tldr: The paper establishes Hölder continuity of the integrated density of states for random Schrödinger operators on Z^d with translation-invariant hopping and i.i.d. absolutely continuous single-site potentials, uniformly in disorder strength.
motivation: Regularity of the integrated density of states (IDS) is central to the spectral theory of disordered systems, underpinning results such as Anderson localization and Lifshitz-tail estimates; the authors aim to extend Hölder continuity to lattice models under weak regularity assumptions on the hopping matrix.
method: Probabilistic/analytic techniques for random Schrödinger operators: the IDS is analyzed via the finite-volume eigenvalue counting function, with a regularity assumption on the hopping matrix controlling eigenvalue variation and yielding Hölder bounds on the distribution of the IDS.
result: Hölder continuity of the IDS is proven up to explicit exponents, with the modulus of continuity independent of the disorder strength.
conclusion: The results provide disorder-uniform regularity of the IDS for a broad class of lattice random Schrödinger operators, useful as an input for localization and transport arguments.

title: A Computational And Experimental Framework For Fourier Optics In Python
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulation of the propagation of light is useful for the design and dimensioning of optical systems. In this paper, we present the basics of propagation simulation using Fourier optics and practical implementation in Python, with a particular emphasis on dimensions. We first verify that our numerical wave-optics simulations maintain correct physical spatial scaling. Next, we benchmark numerical propagation against closed-form analytical formulas for Gaussian beams, lens focusing effects, and grating diffraction. We then show how those simulations can be used to generate diffractive optical elements such as Fresnel zone plates, and we bridge the gap between numerical simulations and experiments by collecting data and recovering phase information using a phase retrieval algorithm.
tldr: The paper presents a Python-based Fourier-optics framework for simulating classical light propagation, validating spatial scaling against analytical Gaussian-beam, lens-focusing, and grating-diffraction results, and closing the loop with phase retrieval on experimental data.
motivation: Designing and dimensioning optical systems requires reliable numerical propagation tools, and practitioners need guidance on maintaining correct physical spatial scaling in wave-optics simulations.
method: The authors implement Fourier-optics propagation in Python, benchmark numerical results against closed-form analytic formulas for Gaussian beams, focusing, and gratings, generate diffractive elements such as Fresnel zone plates, and apply a phase-retrieval algorithm to measured data.
result: The simulations reproduce analytic benchmarks with correct physical scaling, and phase information is successfully recovered from experimental measurements, demonstrating agreement between simulation and experiment.
conclusion: The work provides a practical, well-documented computational toolkit for classical Fourier optics education and optical-system design, though it makes no connection to quantum information science.

title: A Heterogeneous Cpu-gpu Framework For Finite Element Micromagnetic Simulations On Tetrahedral Meshes
authors: Zekai Zheng, Zixuan Cui, Guanghui Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The design of magnetic storage materials relies on repeated micromagnetic simulations. Within each simulation, the demagnetization field evaluation and the sparse linear solve are executed at every time step and together dominate the computational cost. To address these bottlenecks, we develop a heterogeneous CPU-GPU framework that exploits the complementary computational capabilities of the two processors. In the existing AFEMAG solver, developed by Yang et al [J. Comput. Phys. 431 (2021) 110142], computationally intensive boundary integral evaluations and sparse linear solves limit performance. We offload these operations to the GPU while retaining assembly and iteration control on the CPU. We validate the framework using cases from all five [MATH]Mag standard problems, covering quasistatic hysteresis, equilibrium configurations, field-driven dynamics, and spin-transfer-torque dynamics. This approach accelerates simulations across the benchmark suite; notably, for Standard Problem 3 on a mesh of 137,313 nodes, augmenting the CPU with one NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a [MATH] speedup over the CPU-only configuration. The heterogeneous AFEMAG framework thus provides an efficient and practical platform for micromagnetic simulations in the design of magnetic storage materials.
tldr: The paper presents a heterogeneous CPU-GPU framework that accelerates finite-element micromagnetic simulations by offloading demagnetization field evaluation and sparse linear solves to GPUs.
motivation: Micromagnetic simulations for magnetic storage material design are computationally expensive because demagnetization field evaluation and sparse linear solves dominate each time step.
method: The authors extend the AFEMAG finite-element solver by offloading boundary integral evaluations and sparse linear solves to an NVIDIA A100 GPU while keeping assembly and iteration control on the CPU.
result: The framework is validated on all five Micromagnetic Modeling Activity Group standard problems, achieving a notable speedup for Standard Problem 3 on a mesh with 137,313 nodes compared to CPU-only execution.
conclusion: The heterogeneous AFEMAG framework provides an efficient and practical platform for micromagnetic simulations in magnetic storage material design, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: There Is No Binary Linear $[65,9,29]$ Code
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that no binary linear [MATH] code exists, equivalently, that no even binary linear [MATH] code exists. Together with known constructions, this determines [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. A residual-code bound and a known construction also give [MATH]. To prove nonexistence, we associate with a hypothetical even code a quadratic function derived from half the codeword weight modulo [MATH]. Its polar form determines the fourth derivative of a Boolean function of degree at most four. Character sums, weight moments, and the exclusion of weight-[MATH] codewords give upper bounds on the support of this function in seven cases. Restrictions to nondegenerate affine subspaces exclude six cases. In the remaining case, equality would force four distinct coordinate functionals to be identically [MATH] on an affine seven-space, although at most two can have this property. The argument uses published minimum-length results for binary linear codes of dimensions eight and nine.
tldr: The paper proves the nonexistence of a binary linear [65,9,29] code using classical coding-theoretic and Boolean-function techniques.
motivation: Determining the exact minimum distance of binary linear codes for given length and dimension is a fundamental problem in classical coding theory.
method: The authors associate a hypothetical even binary linear code with a quadratic function derived from half the codeword weight modulo 4, then use character sums, weight moments, and restrictions to affine subspaces to rule out all cases.
result: They establish that no binary linear [65,9,29] code exists and determine related minimum-distance values via a residual-code bound and known constructions.
conclusion: This is a pure classical coding-theory nonexistence result with no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: An Explicit Three-Dimensional Dispersing Billiard With Finite Horizon
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct an explicit three-dimensional periodic Lorentz gas whose quotient by the period lattice \(2\Z^3\) has 38 spherical scatterers with rational centers and four rational radii. The scatterers are strictly separated, so the associated dispersing billiard has no corners or cusps. We prove finite horizon by establishing a common blocking margin for every rational direction. A projected-lattice estimate for the face-centered cubic core leaves nine exceptional directions, handled by a finite line-space covering certificate. Simultaneous rational approximation transfers this margin to every direction and yields an explicit upper horizon bound. All finite calculations use exact arithmetic, with verification data and algorithms included. The positive separation and blocking margins also ensure stability under sufficiently small independent perturbations of the centers and radii.
tldr: The paper constructs an explicit three-dimensional periodic Lorentz gas/dispersing billiard with 38 spherical scatterers and proves a finite horizon with an explicit bound.
motivation: Periodic Lorentz gases and dispersing billiards are fundamental models in classical dynamical systems and kinetic theory, and explicit examples with finite horizon are useful for rigorous statistical-physics analysis.
method: The author uses rational scatterer geometry, exact arithmetic, a projected-lattice estimate for the face-centered cubic core, exceptional-direction covering certificates, and simultaneous rational approximation to establish blocking margins.
result: Finite horizon is proven with an explicit upper bound, and the positive separation and blocking margins imply stability under sufficiently small independent perturbations of scatterer centers and radii.
conclusion: This provides a rigorously verified explicit finite-horizon 3D dispersing billiard, contributing to mathematical billiard theory rather than quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Kernel Regression Using Persistence Diagrams
authors: Saksham Aggarwal, James Nichols, Katharine Turner
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistence diagrams are widely used in topological data analysis to summarize topological and geometric structure in data. We study nonparametric regression where inputs are persistence diagrams and outputs are real-valued. Using kernel-based local averaging estimators defined directly over diagram space with Wasserstein distance, we establish consistency and derive bounds on the rate of convergence under suitable assumptions in the [MATH]-theory. We also present computational experiments that demonstrate strong performance of the proposed estimator, particularly in low data regimes.
tldr: The paper develops kernel-based local averaging estimators for nonparametric regression on persistence diagrams using Wasserstein distance and establishes consistency and convergence rates.
motivation: Persistence diagrams are common topological data analysis summaries, but regression with persistence-diagram-valued inputs requires suitable statistical learning methods.
method: The authors define kernel regression estimators directly over diagram space endowed with Wasserstein distance, then prove consistency and derive convergence-rate bounds under suitable assumptions.
result: They establish theoretical guarantees and present computational experiments showing strong performance, especially in low-data settings.
conclusion: The work provides a statistical learning framework for regression from persistence diagrams to real-valued outputs, with both theory and empirical validation.

title: Rigidity And Non-Rigidity Of Disk Pseudo-Rotations Below $c^2$
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For every [MATH], we prove [MATH]-rigidity of area-preserving [MATH] disk pseudo-rotations with non-Brjuno rotation number. At the [MATH] endpoint, every non-Brjuno rotation number of zero exponential type admits non-rigid examples. We also obtain a different rigidity result when the rotation number has positive exponential type: the boundary restriction of every [MATH] pseudo-rotation is rigid and topologically conjugate to a rotation. We show that this boundary conclusion fails in the bi-Lipschitz class by constructing non-rigid examples for every rotation number of finite positive exponential type. The proof of rigidity is based on a finite-information closing theorem under H\"older regularity. For the construction of counterexamples, we use disjoint supports instead of a summable perturbation scheme.
tldr: The paper proves C^0-rigidity of area-preserving disk pseudo-rotations with non-Brjuno rotation numbers below c^2, plus boundary rigidity results and counterexamples showing failure in the bi-Lipschitz class.
motivation: Rigidity of pseudo-rotations is a central question in conservative (symplectic/area-preserving) dynamics, where one asks how strongly the rotation number constrains the dynamics via conjugation to a rotation.
method: The rigidity proof relies on a finite-information closing theorem under Hölder regularity; counterexamples are built using disjointly supported perturbations rather than the usual summable perturbation schemes.
result: C^0-rigidity holds for all non-Brjuno rotation numbers, non-rigid examples exist at the C^0 endpoint for zero-exponential-type numbers, and boundary restrictions of C^0 pseudo-rotations are topologically conjugate to rotations, a conclusion that fails in the bi-Lipschitz class.
conclusion: The work delineates sharp regularity thresholds separating rigid from flexible behavior in area-preserving disk pseudo-rotations, highlighting the role of arithmetic (Brjuno/exponential type) and regularity conditions.

title: Characterizations And Algebraic, Perturbation, And Topological Properties Of $\theta(H)$
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a separable complex Hilbert space, and let [MATH] be the class of bounded operators whose restrictions to every nonzero closed reducing subspace attain their numerical radii. We characterize this property by eigenvalues of suitable self-adjoint parts. For normal operators, membership in [MATH] is equivalent to pure point spectrum and reverse well-ordering of the moduli of eigenvalues. Without normality assumptions, we prove stability under finite orthogonal direct sums using graph subspaces of closed, possibly unbounded, intertwining operators. We give a compact-perturbation criterion in terms of the essential numerical radius and show that an operator remains in [MATH] under every compact perturbation if and only if it is compact. Finally, [MATH] is norm-dense in [MATH] and is norm closed if and only if [MATH] is finite-dimensional.
tldr: The paper characterizes a class of bounded Hilbert-space operators whose restrictions to reducing subspaces attain their numerical radii, and studies algebraic, perturbation, and topological properties of this class.
motivation: The authors aim to understand operators defined by numerical-radius attainment on every nonzero closed reducing subspace, extending spectral and structural characterizations beyond normal operators.
method: They use eigenvalues of self-adjoint parts, graph subspaces of closed intertwining operators, essential numerical radius criteria, and compact-perturbation arguments.
result: For normal operators the property is equivalent to pure point spectrum with reverse well-ordering of eigenvalue moduli; compact-perturbation invariance holds exactly for compact operators; the class is norm-dense and norm-closed only in finite dimensions.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed operator-theoretic classification of this numerical-radius property, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Mutable State In Enrich-by-Need Security Protocol Analysis
authors: Joshua D Guttman, Paul D Rowe, Eben Blaisdell
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security protocol analysis has emphasized message-passing, as this is how different principals interact in authentication, key exchange, and similar functionalities. However, in many protocols a principal also maintains mutable state that limits what actions its local sessions may take; this cross-session state is altered by other local sessions. In this paper we show how to represent this cross-session mutable state in the strand space approach to symbolic protocol analysis, and how to implement the resulting ideas in the Cryptographic Protocol Shapes Analyzer CPSA. The key theory is expressed in two axioms characterizing state, plus protocol-specific rules. It leads to tight, specific characterizations of protocol behavior in relevant cases, and aids in developing correct protocols relying on cross-session mutable state.
tldr: The paper extends strand-space symbolic protocol analysis to model cross-session mutable state and implements this in the CPSA tool.
motivation: Security protocol analysis has mostly focused on message passing, but many protocols also rely on mutable state shared across local sessions, which affects protocol behavior and correctness.
method: The authors represent cross-session mutable state in the strand-space framework using two axioms characterizing state plus protocol-specific rules, and integrate this into the Cryptographic Protocol Shapes Analyzer CPSA.
result: The approach yields tight, specific characterizations of protocol behavior in relevant cases and supports the development of correct protocols that depend on cross-session mutable state.
conclusion: This work improves classical symbolic security protocol analysis by incorporating mutable state, but it does not address quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Verified Netlist-to-RTL Recovery With Llm Agents
authors: Ahmet Efe, Recep Bugra Uludag, Ulya R. Karpuzcu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gate-level netlists circulate among IP integrators and foundries and can be extracted from chips. Reverse engineering them into readable register-transfer-level (RTL) code would help an adversary understand and modify a design, but remains difficult because word-level operations are scattered across many gates. Large language models (LLMs) can write and optimize RTL, but often fail to recover it from a whole netlist. We propose LOCA (LOgic Cone Attack), an LLM-based attack that divides an anonymized netlist into logic cones, has parallel agents rewrite them, and assembles compact RTL. Each cone contains the complete next-state logic of a group of related registers, giving an agent a small, meaningful task. Of five partitioning methods tested, only grouped cones lead to recovery. LOCA keeps only RTL proven equivalent to the netlist and measures its quality by compression. Function-preserving obfuscation does not stop LOCA on the tested designs, whereas unknown keys or hidden cell functions prevent it from proving recovery of the original design. Across 21 model-design pairs, LOCA recovers 17, versus 6 with whole-netlist prompting. Per-run recovery across models rises from 5% to 74%, at a median cost below one dollar with a low-cost model.
tldr: LOCA is an LLM-agent-based attack that recovers readable RTL from anonymized gate-level netlists by partitioning the circuit into grouped logic cones, rewriting each cone with parallel agents, and keeping only formally verified equivalent RTL.
motivation: Gate-level netlists are widely circulated and extractable from chips, so reverse engineering them into RTL would let an adversary understand and modify designs; whole-netlist LLM prompting largely fails at this task.
method: The netlist is split into logic cones each containing the complete next-state logic of related registers, anonymized cones are rewritten in parallel by LLM agents, and the assembled RTL is filtered by equivalence checking against the netlist with compression used as a quality metric.
result: Of five partitioning schemes only grouped cones enable recovery; LOCA recovers 17 of 21 model-design pairs versus 6 with whole-netlist prompting, lifting per-run recovery from 5% to 74% at below one dollar median cost, while function-preserving obfuscation does not prevent recovery but unknown keys or hidden cell functions do.
conclusion: LLM agents with structured circuit partitioning constitute a practical and cheap netlist-to-RTL reverse-engineering threat, underscoring hardware IP security risks.

title: Computational Trust As Intuitionistic Knowledge
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we will argue that the notion of computational trust can be understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification. This approach naturally captures a key aspect of trust: it involves vulnerability. Specifically, it validates the principle that verification leads to trust but does not validate the opposite principle that trust leads to verification. Thus, we can trust on good grounds that some program will perform according to its specification but the program might still fail. We present a simple logic for capturing this notion of computational trust based on constructive modal propositional logic extended with a trust modality, which will be specified in an inferential fashion and by utilizing the proofs-as-programs correspondence.
tldr: The paper argues that computational trust can be modeled as fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification, using a constructive modal logic with a trust modality.
motivation: Trust in computational systems involves vulnerability: verification can justify trust, but trust does not guarantee verification. The authors aim to capture this asymmetry logically.
method: They extend constructive modal propositional logic with a trust modality, specify it inferentially, and use the proofs-as-programs correspondence.
result: The logic validates the principle that verification leads to trust but not the converse, formalizing fallible trust in programs.
conclusion: Computational trust is best understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge, providing a logical foundation for reasoning about trust in software.

title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs For Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing
authors: Pironti Francesco Aurelio, Arena Luigi, Blefari Francesco, Lupinacci Matteo, Romeo Francesco, Maresca Alessio
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.
tldr: ALIoTh is a multi-agent LLM framework for autonomous IoT/IIoT penetration testing using Self-RAG and LangGraph orchestration.
motivation: IoT penetration testing is complex across information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement, motivating an autonomous workflow-driven approach.
method: The framework integrates specialized LLM agents within a Self-RAG architecture and orchestrates them via LangGraph to plan and execute network/device/service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation.
result: The paper describes the design and orchestration of a full-spectrum offensive pipeline leveraging contextual IoT security knowledge and tool documentation.
conclusion: ALIoTh demonstrates how multi-agent LLM systems can automate end-to-end penetration testing in IoT/IIoT environments, though it is outside quantum information research.

title: Direct Measurement Of The On-shot Focal-spot Size Of A Kilojoule-class Petawatt Laser
authors: Ryunosuke Takizawa, Keisuke Takahashi, Yuhei Kawakami, Hiroki Matsubara, Yuga Karaki, Rinya Akematsu, Ryou Oomura, Kai Kimura, Yuki Tamaru, Yasunobu Arikawa, Koji Tsubakimoto, Shinsuke Fujioka
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report a direct, on-shot determination of the focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class, four-beam petawatt laser. Encircled-energy curves were inferred from the energy transmitted around aluminum-coated spheres of varying diameters placed at the focal plane. The 50% encircled-energy diameter D50 of each beam was obtained by fitting a two-component Gaussian mixture with Bayesian inference. With all deformable mirrors optimized in closed loop, the best-corrected alignment beam reached D50 = 34 (+4/-5) um, three times the diffraction limit of 10 um. Under full-power conditions, the thermal distortion of the main amplifier broadened this beam to D50 = 102 (+9/-8) um and reduced its peak intensity ninefold, to 2.2 (+0.6/-0.9) x 10^18 W/cm^2 at 250 J and 1.3 ps. The energy fraction of the narrow component decreased from 68% to 38%. These reference values serve facility users, and a deformable mirror upstream of the pulse compressor, now on one beam only, doubles the on-shot peak intensity.
tldr: The authors directly measure the on-shot focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class four-beam petawatt laser using aluminum-coated spheres at the focal plane and Bayesian fitting of encircled-energy curves.
motivation: Facility users of high-power petawatt lasers need reliable reference values for focal-spot size and peak intensity, which are degraded by thermal distortion of the main amplifier under full-power operation.
method: Encircled-energy curves were inferred from the energy transmitted around aluminum-coated spheres of varying diameters placed at the focal plane; a two-component Gaussian mixture was fitted with Bayesian inference to extract the 50% encircled-energy diameter D50 for each beam.
result: The best-corrected alignment beam reached D50 = 34 (+4/-5) um (three times the 10 um diffraction limit), while under full power thermal distortion broadened it to 102 (+9/-8) um and reduced peak intensity ninefold to 2.2 x 10^18 W/cm^2 at 250 J and 1.3 ps.
conclusion: The reported reference values serve facility users, and a deformable mirror upstream of the pulse compressor is shown to double the on-shot peak intensity on one beam.

title: Real-Time Single-Pixel Imaging Via Exploiting Temporal Mixing: A Unified Calibration And Composite Readout Framework
authors: Jing-Sen Li, En-Rui Zhang, Kan-Xu Jia, Yi-Zhu Zhang, Qian-Qian Bao, Shao-Ying Meng, Xi-Hao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In high-speed optical measurements and computational imaging such as in single-pixel imaging temporal mixing arising from the mismatch between modulation and the electro-optical acquisition chain is conventionally treated as an unmitigated distortion that corrupts measurement orthogonality, breaks compressive sensing priors, fundamentally limits imaging speed, and induces catastrophic reconstruction failure. Here, we establish a transferable, unified calibration and composite-readout framework for single-pixel imaging that systematically repurposes temporal memory from a readout limitation into a powerful measurement resource. Beyond achieving robust high-fidelity recovery, this engineered approach enables cost effective, lower bandwidth configurations to consistently deliver superior image quality compared to higher bandwidth reference setups across diverse operating conditions turning a historical hardware bottleneck into an active imaging advantage. Specifically, target scenes are reconstructed directly from mixed observations without the need to recover individual pattern projections, thereby significantly advancing high-speed and video-rate single-pixel imaging capabilities. Crucially, the transferability of our framework allows calibration routines established on one hardware platform (such as digital micromirror device-based setups) to be readily transferred across different optical systems (such as rotating coding disks), paving the way for calibrated temporal memory as a versatile and generalized measurement paradigm for broader computational imaging.
tldr: The paper reframes temporal mixing in single-pixel imaging, normally treated as a hardware distortion, as an exploitable measurement resource via a unified calibration and composite-readout framework.
motivation: At high speeds, mismatch between spatial modulation and electro-optical readout introduces temporal memory that breaks measurement orthogonality and compressive-sensing priors, causing reconstruction failure and capping imaging speed.
method: The authors build a transferable calibration procedure that characterizes the temporal mixing kernel of the acquisition chain and a composite-readout reconstruction that inverts mixed observations directly, without recovering individual pattern projections, and show it transfers across DMD and rotating-coding-disk platforms.
result: Calibrated lower-bandwidth setups outperform higher-bandwidth reference configurations across operating conditions, yielding robust high-fidelity and video-rate reconstructions.
conclusion: Engineered temporal memory is presented as a generalized measurement paradigm for computational imaging, turning a bandwidth bottleneck into an advantage.

title: Robust Bug Dynamical Low-rank Integrators Based On The Euler-Maruyama Method For Stochastic Differential Equations. Part I: A Closed-moment Approach
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we introduce Euler-Maruyama-based Basis-Update & Galerkin (EM-BUG) dynamical low-rank integrators for stochastic differential equations (SDEs). These integrators extend the standard BUG integrator to the Euler-Maruyama scheme by incorporating diffusion directions into the augmented physical basis and exploiting the second moment to update the physical basis independently of the new Brownian increments. This construction avoids the inversion of the reduced second-moment matrix and allows us to derive convergence estimates that are robust with respect to small eigenvalues. We establish preservation of positive semidefiniteness, exactness with respect to Euler-Maruyama at full rank, and second-moment stability. Strong and weak convergence estimates show that the time-discretization accuracy of the underlying Euler-Maruyama scheme is preserved up to the low-rank approximation error. We also derive Monte Carlo error estimates recovering the standard sampling rate up to the time-discretization and low-rank approximation errors. Numerical experiments on linear SDEs with additive and multiplicative noise support these theoretical results and demonstrate accuracy comparable to the standard BUG integrator.
tldr: The paper introduces Euler-Maruyama-based BUG dynamical low-rank integrators for stochastic differential equations, with robust convergence estimates under small eigenvalues.
motivation: Dynamical low-rank approximation for SDEs needs basis-update schemes that remain stable and accurate when the reduced second-moment matrix is ill-conditioned, which standard approaches handle poorly.
method: The authors extend the BUG (Basis-Update & Galerkin) integrator to the Euler-Maruyama scheme by augmenting the physical basis with diffusion directions and updating it via the second moment, avoiding inversion of the reduced second-moment matrix.
result: They prove preservation of positive semidefiniteness, exactness at full rank, second-moment stability, and strong/weak convergence retaining Euler-Maruyama accuracy up to low-rank error, plus Monte Carlo error estimates; numerics on linear SDEs with additive and multiplicative noise confirm the theory.
conclusion: EM-BUG provides a robust and accurate low-rank integrator for SDEs whose discretization error is controlled even for small eigenvalues, matching standard BUG accuracy in experiments.

title: Small-Gain Analysis Of Robust Event-Triggered Extremum Seeking For Scalar Maps
authors: Victor Hugo Pereira Rodrigues, Tiago Roux Oliveira, Miroslav Krstic, Zhong-Ping Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a sample-and-hold implementation of gradient extremum seeking for a scalar quadratic map in which the control signal is refreshed only when an event occurs. The event generator acts on the demodulated gradient signal as it is actually measured, rather than on its averaged version, and contains a strictly positive offset, following the small-gain philosophy for robust event-triggered control. Rather than invoking averaging theorems, we work directly with the exact dynamics of the parameter estimation error. In the scalar setting, the demodulated gradient has an explicit sinusoidal structure, which is exploited through a change of variables that absorbs the zero-mean oscillatory perturbation, together with a quadratic Lyapunov function and the persistence of excitation of the probing signal. For a sufficiently fast dither, the estimation error is shown to decay exponentially to a residual neighborhood of the origin whose size is quantified by the dither amplitude and frequency, and by the relative threshold and the offset of the event generator. All constants, including the input-to-state stability gain of the extremum seeking loop, the admissible dither frequency and the positive lower bound on the time between two consecutive events, are given in closed form, so that Zeno behavior is excluded. A simulation example illustrates the results.
tldr: The paper analyzes a sample-and-hold event-triggered gradient extremum seeking scheme for a scalar quadratic map, proving exponential decay of the estimation error to a residual neighborhood without invoking averaging theory.
motivation: Event-triggered implementations reduce control updates in extremum seeking, but existing analyses rely on averaging theorems and act on averaged signals; a direct, robust non-averaging analysis with guaranteed inter-event times is desired.
method: Working directly with the exact error dynamics, the authors exploit the explicit sinusoidal structure of the demodulated gradient via a change of variables, a quadratic Lyapunov function, and persistence of excitation, combined with a small-gain, offset-based event generator.
result: For sufficiently fast dither, the estimation error decays exponentially to a residual set whose size is quantified in closed form by the dither amplitude and frequency and by the event generator's relative threshold and offset, with a positive lower bound on inter-event times excluding Zeno behavior.
conclusion: The results provide closed-form robustness and tuning guarantees for event-triggered extremum seeking on scalar quadratic maps, illustrated by a simulation example.

title: The Low-degree Sample Complexity Of Clustering Gaussian Mixtures With More Groups Than Dimensions
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the computational limits of clustering [MATH] observations drawn from a mixture of [MATH] isotropic Gaussian distributions in [MATH], when the number [MATH] of groups is much larger than the dimension [MATH]. In this regime, distance-based and spectral procedures require a squared separation [MATH] of order [MATH]. In contrast, tensor-based procedures cluster at a polylogarithmic separation but need a sample size that is a large polynomial of [MATH], and the low-degree lower bounds known for random centers only show that [MATH] must exceed [MATH]. Focusing on normally distributed centers, we characterize the minimal separation for clustering with low-degree polynomials in the regime [MATH], through a low-degree lower bound and a matching upper bound, up to subpolynomial factors. In particular, for [MATH] with [MATH] a real number, we show that a sample size of the order of [MATH] is required to recover the clustering with subpolynomial separation, and that it suffices when [MATH] is not an integer.
tldr: The paper characterizes the sample complexity of clustering isotropic Gaussian mixtures with more clusters than dimensions using low-degree polynomial algorithms, giving matching low-degree lower and upper bounds on separation.
motivation: In the regime k >> d, distance-based and spectral methods need large squared separation while tensor methods need polynomially large samples and polylogarithmic separation; existing low-degree lower bounds for random centers left a gap.
method: Restricting to normally distributed centers, the authors prove a low-degree lower bound and a matching (up to subpolynomial factors) low-degree upper bound for clustering in the k >> d regime.
result: For k with a real exponent parameter, sample size of order a specified power is necessary to recover the clustering with subpolynomial separation, and sufficient when the parameter is non-integer.
conclusion: The work pins down the minimal separation achievable by low-degree polynomial algorithms for Gaussian mixture clustering, resolving the sample-versus-separation tradeoff in the many-clusters regime.

title: A Fast Iterative Solver For Lopsided Sylvester Matrix Equations
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A generalization of the factored alternating direction implicit algorithm is introduced that makes use of type [MATH] Zolotarev rational functions to apply unequal numbers of left and right shifts. Convergence properties of the algorithm are discussed, as well as a method for computing shift parameters. Several applications are highlighted where the generalized method is useful, including in the solving of a collection of shifted linear systems, for discretizations that involve left and right operators that are not equally amenable to inversion, and for Sylvester matrix equations with differently-sized, differently-structured, or differently-conditioned coefficient matrices.
tldr: The paper introduces a generalized factored alternating direction implicit (ADI) algorithm using Zolotarev rational functions to apply unequal numbers of left and right shifts for solving lopsided Sylvester matrix equations.
motivation: Standard factored ADI solvers assume the left and right operators are equally amenable to inversion and require balanced shift counts, which is inefficient for lopsided problems where the two coefficient matrices differ in size, structure, or conditioning.
method: The authors generalize the factored ADI iteration via type II Zolotarev rational functions that permit asymmetric numbers of left and right shifts, and derive convergence properties plus a scheme for computing the shift parameters.
result: The generalized method is shown to be useful for collections of shifted linear systems, discretizations whose left and right operators are unequally invertible, and Sylvester equations with differently-sized, structured, or conditioned coefficients.
conclusion: The asymmetric Zolotarev-based ADI approach provides a practical and better-conditioned iterative solver for lopsided Sylvester and shifted linear systems arising in numerical discretizations.

title: Variational Integrators For Time-dependent Lagrangian Systems On Lie Groups
authors: Leonardo Colombo, Mar\'ia Emma Eyrea Iraz\'u, David Mart\'in de Diego, Mar\'ia Daniela S\'anchez, Marcela Zuccalli
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, derive their reduced dynamics, and analyze their long-time behavior by backward error analysis. We derive the continuous Euler-Lagrange equations, energy balance, and Noether conservation laws, and construct time-indexed discrete Lagrangians using retractions, with the midpoint-Cayley scheme treated explicitly. On their regularity domains, the resulting phase-space maps are symplectic. For left-invariant discrete Lagrangians, they reduce to Lie-Poisson maps that preserve coadjoint orbits and, when [MATH] is connected, every Casimir function. A variational error analysis establishes second-order accuracy of the midpoint-Cayley method. We also construct an exactly symplectic, projectable extension on [MATH] whose formal modified Hamiltonian is affine in the momentum conjugate to time and admits symmetry reduction. Under uniform analyticity, coefficient bounds, and domain-containment assumptions, optimal truncation yields exponentially accurate interpolation and near-conservation of the modified extended Hamiltonian over exponentially long intervals. For a connected attitude network on [MATH] with damping and uniformly positive, non-increasing coupling weights, we prove local asymptotic stability of the static consensus set for the continuous dynamics and exact preservation of total spatial momentum by the discrete scheme. Numerical experiments on the network and on a time-dependent rigid body on [MATH] illustrate second-order convergence and the extended energy balance.
tldr: The paper develops fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups and analyzes their symplectic, reduction, and long-time conservation properties.
motivation: The authors aim to extend variational integrator theory to time-dependent Lagrangian mechanics on Lie groups, including reduced dynamics and long-time near-conservation guarantees.
method: They derive continuous Euler-Lagrange equations and energy balance, construct retraction-based discrete Lagrangians such as midpoint-Cayley schemes, and use backward error analysis and symplectic reduction theory.
result: The schemes are symplectic on regularity domains, reduce to Lie-Poisson maps preserving coadjoint orbits and Casimirs, achieve second-order accuracy, and exhibit exponentially long near-conservation under analyticity assumptions; attitude-network consensus is also analyzed.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous geometric numerical framework for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, with applications illustrated by a damped attitude network and a time-dependent rigid body.

title: An Explicit Domain-preserving Projected Milstein Scheme With Strong Order One For Stochastic Systems
authors: Xingwei Hu, Yaozhong Hu, Aiguo Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A variety of domain-preserving numerical schemes have been developed for scalar stochastic differential equations and for several classes of multidimensional systems, including those defined on hyperrectangles and positive orthants. To accommodate more general domain constraints, we consider stochastic systems on bounded or unbounded open convex polyhedral domains, where coefficients may exhibit boundary singularities and polynomial growth. Under local regularity, growth and boundary assumptions, we establish well-posedness and integrability estimates for the exact solution. Then we construct an explicit projected Milstein scheme that preserves the domain by applying a Euclidean projection onto a step-size-dependent interior set after each Milstein update. For systems driven by multidimensional commutative noise, we prove strong order-one convergence for the maximum grid error in Lp, for suitable p > 1 and sufficiently small step sizes under additional weighted regularity and stability conditions. The proof combines these integrability estimates with local Milstein consistency, localization and weighted stability, without requiring a priori step-size-uniform moment or boundary inverse-moment bounds for the numerical approximation. Applications to constrained stochastic models and numerical experiments illustrate the observed first-order convergence behavior.
tldr: The paper develops an explicit projected Milstein scheme that preserves convex polyhedral domains for stochastic differential equations and proves strong order-one convergence in Lp.
motivation: Existing domain-preserving numerical schemes cover only scalar SDEs or specific multidimensional domains such as hyperrectangles and positive orthants, so more general convex polyhedral domains with boundary singularities and polynomial-growth coefficients need a well-posedness theory and a provably convergent scheme.
method: The authors establish well-posedness and integrability estimates for the exact solution under local regularity, growth, and boundary assumptions, then construct an explicit Milstein update followed by a Euclidean projection onto a step-size-dependent interior set, analyzing strong order-one convergence via local Milstein consistency, localization, and weighted stability.
result: For systems driven by multidimensional commutative noise, strong order-one convergence of the maximum grid error in Lp is proven for suitable p > 1 and sufficiently small step sizes, without requiring step-size-uniform moment or boundary inverse-moment bounds on the numerical approximation.
conclusion: The scheme provides a rigorous, domain-preserving first-order numerical method for constrained stochastic systems on general convex polyhedral domains, illustrated by applications and numerical experiments.

title: Twisted Enveloping Algebras For Permutation Orbifolds
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate a topological formal calculus for continuous distributions with values in linearly topologized spaces. We apply it here to construct permutation-twisted fields directly from products and branch specializations. For a vertex operator algebra [MATH], the key structural observation is that modes of tensors with at most one non-vacuum factor topologically generate the permutation-twisted enveloping algebra. Combining this observation with the calculus and [MATH], we obtain an explicit isomorphism [MATH] for an [MATH]-cycle [MATH], with grading and canonical filtrations rescaled by [MATH]. For arbitrary permutations, the cycle factors are rescaled before taking their degreewise completed tensor product.
tldr: The paper constructs permutation-twisted fields and twisted enveloping algebras for vertex operator algebras using a topological formal calculus.
motivation: It aims to develop a formal calculus for continuous distributions valued in linearly topologized spaces and apply it to construct permutation-twisted fields from products and branch specializations.
method: The authors introduce a topological formal calculus and show that modes of tensors with at most one non-vacuum factor topologically generate the permutation-twisted enveloping algebra.
result: They obtain an explicit isomorphism for cycle permutations with grading and canonical filtrations rescaled, and extend it to arbitrary permutations via completed tensor products of rescaled cycle factors.
conclusion: The work provides an algebraic construction of permutation-twisted enveloping algebras in the setting of vertex operator algebras, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: When And Why Can Integral Constraints Improve The Accuracy Of Physics-informed Neural Networks?
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.
tldr: The paper analyzes when integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks for solving PDEs via stability estimates.
motivation: Integral constraints are empirically known to improve PINN accuracy, but the mathematical reasons for this improvement are not well understood.
method: The author derives stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints for several PDEs and compares their control over error components, supported by numerical experiments.
result: Integral constraints restore uniform control over certain error components in parameter regimes where the standard loss has weak control, explaining observed accuracy differences.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical interpretation of when and why integral constraints benefit PINNs, with numerical evidence consistent with the theory.

title: Operator Generated Topologies And The Krein Property
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a Banach space and [MATH] a subspace separating the points of [MATH]. We say that [MATH] has the Krein property if the [MATH]-closed convex hull of every norm-bounded [MATH]-compact set is [MATH]-compact. We show that this property passes from [MATH] to every subspace between [MATH] and its sequential weak[MATH] closure in [MATH], and that the closed convex hulls do not change. In particular, it passes to the smallest [MATH]-invariant space [MATH] whenever the operator [MATH] is a pointwise [MATH]-limit of a sequence of [MATH]-continuous operators; for nets this fails in general and holds under a double limit condition. As a source of spaces with the Krein property we show that the Mackey topologies [MATH] and [MATH] are complete if the identity of [MATH] is suitably approximated by a sequence of operators whose adjoints map [MATH] into [MATH]; in particular, [MATH] and [MATH] are complete for every [MATH]-semigroup on a Banach space [MATH] with sun dual [MATH]. The results are applied to the history space [MATH] of delay equations with infinite delay, where every space of bounded measures containing [MATH] has the Krein property.
tldr: A pure functional-analysis paper establishing inheritance and completeness results for the Krein property of Banach spaces and their subspaces, with an application to history spaces of delay equations.
motivation: The authors aim to understand when the closed convex hulls of compact sets remain compact in weak or Mackey topologies, a technical question arising in the duality theory of operator semigroups and infinite-delay equations.
method: Abstract Banach-space and duality arguments: they show the Krein property passes to subspaces between a space and its sequential weak*-closure, characterize settings where Mackey topologies are complete via approximation of the identity by operators with adjoints preserving the predual, and treat nets versus sequences via a double-limit condition.
result: The Krein property is preserved under the described subspace constructions and holds for all spaces of bounded measures containing the history space of infinite-delay equations; completeness of the Mackey topologies is obtained for semigroups on Banach spaces with sun duals.
conclusion: The work provides general structural criteria for the Krein property and Mackey completeness, but remains entirely within abstract functional analysis with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: A Weakly Singular Volterra Integral Equation And The Fractional Lyapunov Asymptotic Stability Theorem
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the weakly singular Volterra integral equation V(t) = A - (1/Gamma(alpha)) int_0^t (t-s)^{alpha-1} h(|V(s)|) ds, t >= 0, where alpha in (0,1), A > 0 and h is a class-K function. This equation arises as the scalar reduction of fractional-order Lyapunov inequalities through the fractional variation-of-constants formula. We prove that it admits a unique global solution V with 0 < V(t) <= A, that V is non-increasing, and that V(t) tends to 0 as t goes to infinity, under the pure class-K hypothesis on h. If, in addition, h is locally Holder continuous on (0,infinity) with exponent beta > 1 - alpha, then the rescaled function W(t) := V(t^{1/alpha}) is of class C^1 on [0,infinity) and satisfies W'(t) <= 0. We determine the optimal regularity of the solution, which is alpha-Holder continuous with the sharp expansion V(t) = A - h(A) t^alpha / Gamma(alpha+1) + o(t^alpha) at the origin, and its sharp decay rate h(V(t)) ~ A t^{-alpha} / Gamma(1-alpha) as t goes to infinity. In the power case h(x) ~ kappa x^p one has V(t) ~ (A/(kappa Gamma(1-alpha)))^{1/p} t^{-alpha/p}. As an application, we give a complete proof of the fractional-order Lyapunov asymptotic stability theorem of Li, Chen and Podlubny (Theorem 11, Automatica 45 (2009), 1965-1969) under the general class-K hypothesis, a case not covered by the linear, power-law and convex arguments available in the literature. This theorem plays for fractional-order stability theory the role of Lyapunov's classical theorem for ODEs, and its proof closes a gap that has been open since the theorem first appeared. We further show that the Caputo inequality C_0D_t^alpha V(t) <= -c V^p(t) with 0 < p < 1 implies Mittag-Leffler stability of V, yet neither entails nor precludes finite-time decay to zero, in contrast with the integer-order criterion V'(t) <= -c V^p(t), which entails finite-time decay to zero.
tldr: The paper proves global well-posedness, regularity, and sharp decay for a weakly singular Volterra integral equation arising from fractional-order Lyapunov inequalities, and applies this to close a gap in the fractional Lyapunov asymptotic stability theorem.
motivation: Fractional-order Lyapunov stability theorems are widely used but the general class-K case lacked a complete proof; the authors reduce the stability question to a scalar weakly singular Volterra inequality.
method: They analyze V(t)=A-(1/Gamma(alpha))∫_0^t (t-s)^{alpha-1} h(|V(s)|) ds for class-K h, prove uniqueness and monotonicity, establish optimal Holder regularity and sharp short-time/long-time asymptotics, and apply the result to Caputo fractional inequalities.
result: The equation has a unique non-increasing global solution 0<V(t)≤A tending to 0, with sharp expansion at the origin and sharp decay h(V(t))~A t^{-alpha}/Gamma(1-alpha); the fractional Lyapunov asymptotic stability theorem of Li, Chen, and Podlubny is proved under the general class-K hypothesis.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous analytical foundation for fractional-order Lyapunov stability and clarifies differences from integer-order finite-time stability criteria.

title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A learning-assisted framework for Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) methods is developed in which lightweight online prediction is used to support, rather than replace, the classical optimization process. The proposed approach retains the standard two-term NCG structure and introduces two independent online extreme learning machine models. The first model predicts an NCG coefficient during restart recovery or when persistent stagnation is detected, whereas the second model is used only after a line-search failure in finite precision arithmetic to propose a bounded correction to the deterministic fallback step size. Neural predictions are accepted only when they satisfy deterministic numerical safeguards, including descent, scale, and out-of-distribution requirements; otherwise, the corresponding deterministic recovery or fallback mechanism is retained. Both learning models are updated online using quantities already generated along the optimization trajectory and therefore require no additional function or gradient evaluations for training. These learning frameworks are applied to six well-known classical NCG methods, producing corresponding low-storage learning-assisted variants with deterministic safeguards. Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst test problems show improved robustness for all six variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs. A PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example further illustrates the potential of the proposed approach to reduce evaluation costs and computational time for problems with expensive function and gradient evaluations. These findings suggest that restricted online learning can improve the robustness and computational performance of classical NCG methods while preserving their low-storage structure and deterministic optimization safeguards, and is particularly promising when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.
tldr: The paper develops learning-assisted nonlinear conjugate gradient methods with online extreme learning machine predictors guarded by deterministic numerical safeguards.
motivation: Classical nonlinear conjugate gradient methods can suffer from restart recovery, stagnation, and finite-precision line-search failures, while fully replacing them with learned optimizers risks losing robustness and low-storage guarantees.
method: It retains the standard two-term NCG structure and adds two online extreme learning machine models: one predicts an NCG coefficient during restart/stagnation, and another proposes a bounded fallback step-size correction after line-search failure, with predictions accepted only if deterministic numerical safeguards are satisfied.
result: Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst problems show improved robustness for six classical NCG variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs, and a PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example illustrates potential cost and time reductions for expensive evaluations.
conclusion: Restricted online learning can improve NCG robustness and computational performance while preserving low-storage structure and deterministic safeguards, especially when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.

title: Signed, Valid, And Unauthorized: Authority Closure At The Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols And Crypto Wallets
authors: Shengwei You, Aditya Joshi, Andrey Kuehlkamp, Jarek Nabrzyski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.
tldr: The paper introduces 'authority closure' as a formal property of signed wallet objects used by autonomous software agents in stablecoin payments, and implements Closure, a wallet-side checker that verifies signed objects cannot enable transfers outside the buyer's mandate.
motivation: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins, but the object a wallet signs may permit transfer sequences whose effects go beyond the fields the buyer approved; field matching or single-payment simulation fails to catch these latent authorizations.
method: The authors define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences enabled by holding a signed object, characterize when wallet objects satisfy the mandate property, and build Closure, a checker covering 13 families of signed objects, evaluated on 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs plus local x402 client checkouts.
result: 265 objects with observed violations passed both field-and-expiry checks and an address allow-list, while Closure rejected all 1,680 violating objects and accepted the 450 valid ones, with median decision times of at most 12 microseconds per family.
conclusion: Wallet-side enforcement of authority closure closes a trust-boundary gap in agent commerce protocols, providing fast, sound pre-signing validation of signed objects against buyer mandates.

title: Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization For Bitcoin Custody
authors: Jian Cui (university Of Illinois Urbana-Champaign), Rui Zhu (yale University), Haixu Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A compromised cryptocurrency withdrawal backend can request signatures on unauthorized payments. Previously signed transactions may remain spendable after pause or become spendable again after a reorganization. Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization (RBWA) orders permits against pause in a replicated journal and restores exposure when its closing evidence disappears from Bitcoin's active chain. An optional route delays large payouts and permits independent cold recovery. Direct payments confirm in one block on regtest, and staged payments confirm in three or seven at delays of two or six. After rollback, a replayed recovery can win or lose to an already exported mature payout. Authenticated receipts can revoke one signing lease in a shared wallet. In matched synthetic schedules, probes reduce permits through compromised leases from 20 to 9 out of 33, with one false fence. Two held-out HTTP workloads find equal fixed-threshold precision for boosted audit and probe-augmented detectors. The audit fields already expose the probe authentication outcome. Live tests verify an exact maintenance exception and add a file marker as a distinct source. The marker fences a compromised lease that RPC-only audit misses. Audit with the same file-read evidence also fences a reader who bypasses the probe. The results tie the benefit of active probing to which evidence the operator can obtain.
tldr: The paper proposes Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization (RBWA), a replicated-journal protocol that binds Bitcoin withdrawal permits to pause events and restores exposure when closing evidence vanishes from the active chain.
motivation: A compromised cryptocurrency withdrawal backend can request signatures on unauthorized payments, and previously signed transactions may become spendable again after chain reorganizations, so custody systems need authorization schemes that react to chain state.
method: Permits are ordered against pause in a replicated journal, with optional delayed routing for large payouts and independent cold recovery; evaluation uses regtest confirmation tests, synthetic matched schedules with probes, held-out HTTP workloads, and live maintenance-exception tests.
result: Probes reduce permits issued through compromised leases from 20 to 9 out of 33 with one false fence, and a file-marker evidence source fences a compromised lease that RPC-only audit misses, while both workloads show equal fixed-threshold precision.
conclusion: The benefit of active probing depends on which audit evidence the operator can obtain, tying protocol security to available evidence sources in Bitcoin custody deployments.

title: Proof Checking Continuous Reachability
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a proof format and proof checker for certifying reachability computations of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with polynomial vector fields. Establishing a proof checking framework for certifying ODE reachability is similar to the checking of UNSAT proofs for propositional satisfiability solving, but it is even more important due to the challenges inherent in dealing with ODEs, and even more challenging due to the numerical nature of ODE reachability algorithms. The proofs are expressed in differential dynamic logic (dL), and can be independently verified with symbolic theorem provers for dL (e.g. KeYmaeraX). Such proofs are naturally generated by reachability algorithms based on Taylor models, a popular technique to obtain rigorous bounds on approximations of ODEs. This paper proves the completeness of such proofs - if an approximation was correctly computed by some (possibly untrusted) reachability algorithm via Taylor models, then a corresponding proof in dL can be automatically generated and checked to be correct in dL's proof calculus. A dedicated proof checker is implemented in Lean4 for improved performance, which is capable of formally verifying benchmarks in the ARCH competition.
tldr: The paper introduces a proof format and Lean4 proof checker for certifying ODE reachability computations generated via Taylor-model methods in differential dynamic logic.
motivation: Certifying numerical reachability computations for ODEs is important because such algorithms are complex, numerical, and potentially untrusted, analogous to UNSAT proof checking in SAT solving.
method: Proofs are expressed in differential dynamic logic and independently verified with symbolic theorem provers such as KeYmaeraX; the authors prove completeness for Taylor-model-generated proofs and implement a dedicated checker in Lean4.
result: The framework can automatically generate and check dL proofs for correctly computed Taylor-model reachability approximations, and the Lean4 checker formally verifies ARCH competition benchmarks.
conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous proof-checking framework for continuous reachability, improving trust in ODE reachability results, but it is outside the listed quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems research directions.

title: Fundamentals For Binary Classification Under Label Noise
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This chapter surveys fundamental results for binary classification under label noise. Binary classification under label noise involves training models on datasets where class labels are partially incorrect, leading to degraded performance and misclassification. We distinguish poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalize random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. These models capture different adversarial strengths and data-generation realities. We then highlight some core ideas and representative results. In particular, we explain why random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses and thus supports learning using the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, how sample complexity depends on the noise rate, and why learning algorithms often require an upper bound on the corruption level, as well as how such a bound may be estimated from data in the case of random classification noise. We also discuss computational aspects of ERM under noise and present a canonical negative result technique -- the method of induced distributions -- within the malicious noise model where the adversary has more power and may affect not only the label of an example but also the instance. We conclude with pointers to related work and a taxonomy that organizes classical label-noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.
tldr: A survey chapter on fundamental results for binary classification under label noise within the PAC learning framework.
motivation: Label noise in training data degrades model performance, so a systematic overview of noise models and their learnability guarantees is needed.
method: Formalizes random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious noise in the PAC framework and reviews representative results, sample complexity bounds, and the method of induced distributions.
result: Explains why ERM works under random classification noise, how sample complexity scales with noise rate, when an upper bound on corruption is required, and presents a canonical hardness technique for malicious noise.
conclusion: Provides a taxonomy of classical label-noise models via the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens along with pointers to related work.

title: VisualJevBench: A Benchmark And Black-Box Attacks For Visual Typed Decision Models
authors: Li Zeng, Yeqi Zeng, Hengkai Liang, Shiguo Wang, Meng Xie, Zeyu Ye, Jinheng Zhang, Xianlong Wang, Ziqi Zhou, Hangtao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return structured decisions instead of generating free-text responses, enabling fast and cheap decisions in real-world applications. Recent support for image inputs extends Jev, a representative TDM, to visual decision-making. We refer to this setting as Visual Jev. However, red teaming of Visual Jev leaves two gaps: a systematic evaluation of direct image manipulations is lacking, and universal visual attacks remain underexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce VisualJevBench, a benchmark for evaluating the adversarial robustness of Visual Jev. It comprises 800 images and 3,200 questions across eight scenarios and four visual attack surfaces: typographic manipulation, visual evidence spoofing, target selection interference, and geometric transformation. We also introduce Adaptive Black-Box Parameter Search (ABPS), a lightweight framework that uses typed-output feedback to find effective image manipulations. ABPS supports both image-specific attacks and universal attacks that transfer to unseen images and tasks in new scenarios without further optimization. Extensive experiments on jev-1.14.0 show that image-specific attacks achieve an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 69.6%, while universal attacks achieve an average ASR of 33.15% on unseen images. Geometric transformations achieve an average ASR of 40.09% in cross-scenario transfer.
tldr: VisualJevBench introduces a benchmark of 800 images and 3,200 questions to evaluate adversarial robustness of Visual Jev typed decision models, plus a black-box attack framework (ABPS) achieving up to 69.6% attack success.
motivation: Typed decision models such as Jev now accept image inputs, but red teaming of this 'Visual Jev' setting lacks systematic evaluation of direct image manipulations and universal visual attacks.
method: The authors build a benchmark spanning eight scenarios and four visual attack surfaces (typographic manipulation, visual evidence spoofing, target selection interference, geometric transformation) and propose Adaptive Black-Box Parameter Search (ABPS), which uses typed-output feedback to optimize image-specific and universal attacks.
result: On jev-1.14.0, image-specific attacks reach up to 69.6% ASR, universal attacks average 33.15% ASR on unseen images, and geometric transformations achieve 40.09% ASR in cross-scenario transfer.
conclusion: Visual Jev models are substantially vulnerable to both targeted and transferable black-box visual attacks, highlighting the need for robustness evaluation and defenses in structured-decision LLM systems.

title: Passing Npcr Without Diffusion: Exact Signatures, A Detection Benchmark And An Audit Of Published Image Ciphers
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: NPCR, the share of ciphertext bytes changed by a one-pixel plaintext change, is reported for nearly every image cipher as evidence of diffusion, with 99.61% the target. Several mechanisms produce values near it, and the mean does not say which. We separate three regimes: no propagation, one round of forward and backward chaining linear over addition or XOR, and independent ciphertexts. For the second an exact count applies.
