After a least-significant-bit change its mean asymptotically matches the independent-ciphertext reference, while its spread without cancellation is about five to twenty times larger. In simulation, the one-sided NPCR test of Wu, Noonan and Agaian flags one-round additive, mixed and S-box chaining in 2-4% of papers; read in both directions, the same five values flag at least 99.9%. Two-sided testing does the detecting; the spread and the other signatures help diagnose the structure. We then audit twenty-one published schemes. The count matches a reimplementation of one published diffusion layer on every trial and accounts for its reported table, the signatures show two schemes whose printed specifications cannot produce their reported values, and find that three of our own report plain-versus-cipher values and fall to two chosen images; ten more change their encryption material with the plaintext or per encryption, so their NPCR mostly reflects that change. A released checker applies the signatures to published tables, showing what a table measures within stated assumptions; it does not certify security.
tldr: Analyzes NPCR diffusion metrics in image ciphers, distinguishes propagation regimes, and audits published encryption schemes.
motivation: NPCR is widely reported as evidence of diffusion in image ciphers, but values near 99.61% can arise from different mechanisms, so the mean alone is ambiguous.
method: The paper separates no-propagation, one-round chaining, and independent-ciphertext regimes; derives exact counts for one-round chaining; tests detection behavior in simulation; and audits 21 published schemes with a released checker.
result: One-sided NPCR tests detect weakly, while two-sided testing detects strongly; signatures help diagnose structure and reveal inconsistencies in several published schemes.
conclusion: The checker interprets what published NPCR tables measure under stated assumptions, but it does not certify cryptographic security.

title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine For System-Level Monitoring Of Agents
authors: Meghana Aparna Sistla, Alaia Solko-Breslin, Somesh Jha, Aditya Kanade, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.
tldr: Tether is a Lean 4-embedded DSL framework that sandboxes AI agent actions, infers abstract semantics from system calls, and enforces stateful information-flow, access-control, and network policies with formally verified global security invariants.
motivation: Autonomous agents executing arbitrary shell commands can leak data or persist malicious changes, and existing defenses either rely on unverified LLM monitors or stateless policy layers that miss multi-step data flows and side effects like network calls inside Python scripts.
method: Each proposed action is run in an ephemeral isolated sandbox; observed system calls are abstracted into action semantics, over which stateful policies written in an embedded Lean 4 DSL are checked, allowing formal verification of global invariants such as preventing network access after reading a sensitive file.
result: Evaluated on realistic coding-agent benchmarks with benign and adversarial trajectories, a single shared policy blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while keeping benign false positives under 5%.
conclusion: Formally verified, stateful, sandbox-based policy enforcement offers provable safety guarantees for agentic systems that stateless or LLM-based monitors cannot provide.

title: MetaScanner: An Empirical Study And Proactive Defense Against Deceptive Ui Attacks In Social Vr
authors: Junhee Lee, Seungwon Woo, Minseok Kim, Jongseop Kim, Kiyoung Kim, Hwanjo Heo, Jinwoo Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social virtual reality (VR) platforms have surged in popularity but continue to face significant security challenges, including privacy invasion and user manipulation. Yet, the security risks posed by deceptive content remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce four novel deceptive UI attacks that covertly manipulate social VR users into performing unintended actions without their awareness. We show how adversarial content creators can embed seemingly benign scripts and interactive elements within carefully designed virtual worlds, deceiving users into unknowingly carrying out harmful behaviors. We implemented these attacks on VRChat, a leading social VR platform, and an IRB-approved user study involving 30 participants confirmed their effectiveness. To mitigate these threats, we propose MetaScanner, a proactive analysis system that efficiently scans virtual world assets, including scripts and interactive objects, to identify suspicious or deceptive elements before users are exposed to them. We demonstrate that MetaScanner can successfully detect all threats in test worlds where the four attack scenarios were implemented. Additionally, MetaScanner shows its lightweight nature, with an average scanning time of 5 seconds across 38 real-world assets.
tldr: The paper introduces four deceptive UI attacks in social VR platforms and proposes MetaScanner, a proactive asset-scanning defense system.
motivation: Social VR platforms are increasingly popular but the security risks of deceptive content within them remain largely unexplored.
method: The authors design four novel deceptive UI attack scenarios, implement them on VRChat, validate them with an IRB-approved 30-participant user study, and build MetaScanner to statically scan world scripts and interactive objects for suspicious elements.
result: All four attacks were effective on real users, and MetaScanner detected all threats in test worlds while scanning 38 real-world assets in about 5 seconds on average.
conclusion: Deceptive UI attacks pose a real threat in social VR, and lightweight proactive asset scanning can mitigate them before users are exposed.

title: Erasing The Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage And Concept Erasure In Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
authors: Haijun He, Fei Li, Donghong Ji, Junjun He
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.
tldr: The paper proves a conflict between global and task-conditional linear guardedness in shared foundation-model embeddings and proposes TC-LEACE to enforce task-conditional erasure.
motivation: Medical-image embeddings shared for downstream tasks may leak sensitive attributes, and standard global concept-erasure methods may fail to prevent task-conditional leakage.
method: The authors derive a theoretical impossibility result, analyze utility costs, introduce Task-Conditional LEACE as a closed-form variant of LEACE, and evaluate it on CelebA attributes and hospital chest radiographs.
result: Conditional leakage persists after LEACE across vision foundation models, increases with label association strength, and is also detectable in diagnosis strata for chest-tube status; TC-LEACE recovers most task utility while bounding conditional leakage.
conclusion: Global erasure can be insufficient for sensitive-attribute protection in shared embeddings, and task-conditional erasure offers a more targeted trade-off between privacy leakage and utility.

title: Distortion In Online Voting
authors: Mohammadhossein Ghasemi, Masoud Seddighin, Saeed Seddighin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We initiate the study of distortion in online voting, a framework that bridges computational social choice and online algorithms. In contrast to the classical offline setting, where the full election instance is known in advance, we consider a dynamic environment where a fixed set of voters is present from the beginning, but alternatives arrive sequentially over time. Upon each arrival, a mechanism must immediately and irrevocably decide whether to retain the currently selected candidate or switch to the newly arriving one, operating solely on the partial ordinal rankings induced by the underlying cardinal preferences. We provide upper and lower bounds for deterministic and randomized mechanisms under two standard cardinal preference frameworks. Utilitarian framework: For deterministic mechanisms under adversarial arrival order, we establish an [MATH] lower bound and give an matching online algorithm with distortion at most [MATH]. For randomized rules, we introduce regularity, which allows any regular, order-independent offline randomized rule to be converted into an online rule with the same expected distortion. The Harmonic voting rule satisfies this property, yielding online distortion [MATH]. Metric framework: For deterministic mechanisms, maintaining an alternative within a [MATH]-weighted uncovered set guarantees distortion [MATH]. We show that matching-based offline rules achieving distortion [MATH] cannot be directly implemented online. We establish a lower bound of [MATH], even with three alternatives, and a matching upper bound for three alternatives and any number of voters. For randomized mechanisms, regularity gives an online distortion of [MATH] via Random Dictatorship.
tldr: The paper initiates the study of distortion in online voting, where alternatives arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected irrevocably based on partial ordinal rankings.
motivation: Classical distortion studies assume the full election instance is known offline, but many practical voting settings involve alternatives arriving over time, requiring online decision-making under partial preference information.
method: The authors analyze deterministic and randomized online voting mechanisms under utilitarian and metric cardinal preference frameworks, deriving upper and lower bounds and introducing a regularity condition for converting offline randomized rules to online rules.
result: They establish tight or matching bounds in several settings, including an online algorithm matching a lower bound in the utilitarian deterministic case, and show that some good offline matching-based rules cannot be directly implemented online.
conclusion: Online voting introduces new distortion trade-offs not present offline, and regularity provides a useful bridge for designing randomized online mechanisms with bounded distortion.

title: Closing Gaps In Temporal Fair Division For Chores
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible chores that must be assigned in a prescribed order. The complete instance is known in advance, but assignments cannot be changed. Temporal envy-freeness up to one chore (TEF1) requires envy-freeness up to one chore after every arrival. For goods, TEF1 allocations need not exist, and deciding whether one exists is NP-hard. For chores, Elkind et al. (AAMAS 2025) showed that TEF1 allocations exist for two agents, but left open whether they always exist, conjecturing that they do not, and whether deciding their existence is hard. We resolve both questions, confirming the conjecture in a strong form: for every [MATH] and every finite factor, some [MATH]-agent instance admits no allocation satisfying TEF1 even up to that factor. This holds even when all agents have the same multiset of individual chore costs, with nine chores sufficing for three agents. Deciding TEF1 existence is NP-complete for every fixed [MATH], even when all costs lie within a factor [MATH] of one another, where [MATH] is the number of chores. Instances without TEF1 allocations exist arbitrarily close to the uniform cost matrix with [MATH] chores, and just nineteen for three agents. We then relate fairness to social cost. Even when a TEF1 allocation is supplied, minimizing social cost subject to TEF1 admits no polynomial-time approximation within any factor polynomial in the number of chores unless P[MATH]NP, already for three agents with strictly positive normalized costs. In contrast, for every fixed number of agents, we give an FPTAS for the optimal temporal EF1 factor, the smallest factor up to which TEF1 can be satisfied, whose output has social cost no larger than that of the cheapest allocation attaining this factor. Thus a slight relaxation of fairness permits a social-cost guarantee that, unless P[MATH]NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can provide under exact TEF1.
tldr: The paper resolves open questions on temporal envy-freeness up to one chore (TEF1) for indivisible chores, showing non-existence in strong form and NP-completeness of deciding existence, plus social-cost approximation results.
motivation: Temporal fair division of goods and chores is a central problem in computational social choice; for chores, existence of TEF1 allocations was known only for two agents, leaving open whether they always exist and whether the decision problem is hard.
method: The author constructs counterexample instances for arbitrary numbers of agents and any multiplicative factor, proves NP-completeness of TEF1 existence via reduction, and analyzes social cost minimization under TEF1 constraints, deriving hardness of approximation and an FPTAS for the optimal temporal EF1 factor.
result: TEF1 allocations fail to exist for every number of agents and every finite approximation factor (nine chores suffice for three agents); deciding TEF1 existence is NP-complete for every fixed number of agents; minimizing social cost subject to TEF1 admits no polynomial-time approximation unless P=NP, while an FPTAS exists for the relaxed optimal EF1 factor.
conclusion: Slight relaxations of temporal fairness are necessary and sufficient to recover tractable social-cost guarantees, sharply separating exact TEF1 from its approximate variants.

title: Mateability Of Fuchsian Lattices With Polynomials, And Failure Of Algebraicity
authors: Yusheng Luo, Mahan Mj, Sabyasachi Mukherjee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that all Fuchsian lattices, with the possible exceptions of those associated with compact orbifolds of type (0,3) and (1,1), can be mated with complex polynomials, providing the first examples of such combinations beyond genus-zero orbifolds. We also present the first construction of matings between simply degenerate Kleinian groups and polynomial maps. These matings are realized as holomorphic, though not necessarily algebraic, correspondences, demonstrating that Fatou's vision of unifying Kleinian group actions and polynomial dynamics can be fulfilled in the wider setting of transcendental correspondences. We achieve this by generalizing the orbit equivalence mating framework introduced in our earlier work. Specifically, we use pinching and acceleration techniques to construct a new class of piecewise M\"obius covering maps of the circle that are orbit equivalent to Fuchsian groups. By mating these circle coverings with polynomials, we construct degenerate polynomial-like maps whose analytic continuations yield the desired correspondences. The quality of this orbit equivalence plays a crucial role in the mating description, as well as in governing whether the resulting correspondences are algebraic.
tldr: The paper proves new mating results between Fuchsian lattices and complex polynomials, realized as holomorphic correspondences.
motivation: It aims to extend Fatou's program of unifying Kleinian group actions and polynomial dynamics beyond genus-zero orbifolds and algebraic correspondences.
method: The authors generalize orbit-equivalence mating by using pinching and acceleration to construct piecewise Möbius circle coverings orbit equivalent to Fuchsian groups, then mate these with polynomials.
result: They show that almost all Fuchsian lattices can be mated with complex polynomials except possibly compact orbifolds of type (0,3) and (1,1), and give the first matings of simply degenerate Kleinian groups with polynomial maps.
conclusion: The constructed correspondences are holomorphic but not necessarily algebraic, showing that Fatou's vision can be fulfilled in the broader setting of transcendental correspondences.

title: Integer Programming Strategies For The Snake-in-the-Box Problem
authors: Tim Kunt, Thorsten Koch, Hyejun Park
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a selection of Integer Programming (IP) strategies for the Snake-in-the-Box problem, which asks for the longest induced path in the [MATH]-dimensional hypercube. Current records are based on sophisticated, exhaustive searches, with optimality proven only for instances up to dimension 8, motivating our study of IP formulations. We address symmetries and potential strengthenings. With the smallest open instance having as few as 512 binary decision variables, the proposed IPs offer a challenging and intriguing combinatorial problem. In addition, we extend the problem to higher-dimensional grid graphs and provide solutions for unexplored and unsolved instances.
tldr: This paper develops integer programming strategies for finding long induced paths in hypercubes and higher-dimensional grid graphs.
motivation: The Snake-in-the-Box problem is a classical combinatorial optimization problem where optimal solutions are known only up to dimension 8, motivating new exact and heuristic formulations.
method: The authors propose several Integer Programming formulations, address symmetries, and discuss potential strengthenings for the problem.
result: The formulations are applied to small open instances with 512 binary variables and extended to higher-dimensional grid graphs, yielding solutions for previously unexplored cases.
conclusion: The work provides a new IP-based approach to a challenging combinatorial problem, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Herz-type Besov And Triebel-Lizorkin Spaces With General Weights
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new family of function spaces of generalized smoothness that encompasses the classical Besov and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces, their weighted counterparts, as well as Herz-type Besov and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces. We provide a characterization of these spaces via the [MATH]-transform in the sense of Frazier and Jawerth, and establish the corresponding Sobolev embeddings. Furthermore, we obtain smooth atomic and molecular decompositions for these spaces. Our approach relies on several new maximal inequalities.
tldr: The paper introduces and studies new Herz-type Besov and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces with general weights, including transform characterizations, Sobolev embeddings, and atomic/molecular decompositions.
motivation: The authors aim to unify classical Besov/Triebel-Lizorkin spaces, weighted variants, and Herz-type spaces within a general framework of smoothness spaces.
method: The approach uses the phi-transform of Frazier and Jawerth, new maximal inequalities, and smooth atomic and molecular decomposition techniques.
result: The paper provides characterizations via phi-transforms, establishes Sobolev embeddings, and obtains atomic and molecular decompositions for the new family of function spaces.
conclusion: This work extends the theory of generalized smoothness spaces and offers tools for further analysis in harmonic analysis and function space theory.

title: Attacks And Defenses In Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems With Hop-by-Hop Task Decomposition And Delegation
authors: Matthew D. Laws, Maria Lazou, Alina Oprea, Cristina Nita-Rotaru
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. Agents autonomously decompose tasks, execute subtasks and delegate remaining work to peers, enabling scalability and eliminating single points of failure. However, decentralization also introduces significant security challenges, as no single entity has complete visibility into task execution or the authority to enforce correct behavior across agents. In this paper, we systematize threats from malicious agents in decentralized multi-agent systems and propose mitigation techniques. We first design and evaluate attacks against integrity, availability, and confidentiality, demonstrating that a single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, respectively, and exfiltrate up to 94% of relevant prior tasks from benign agents. We then present a cryptographic protocol that produces an irrefutable verified execution trace of every action taken in the system and develop an auditor that analyzes these traces to detect and attribute malicious behavior. Evaluations on HiddenBench using gpt-6.1-sol and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 show that our protocol incurs negligible latency overhead, while the auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks, including those that comply with the protocol.
tldr: The paper systematizes attacks and defenses for decentralized multi-agent LLM systems, proposing a cryptographic execution-trace protocol and auditor to detect and attribute malicious agent behavior.
motivation: Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems offer scalability and eliminate single points of failure, but lack centralized visibility and enforcement, creating security vulnerabilities from malicious agents.
method: The authors design and evaluate integrity, availability, and confidentiality attacks, then introduce a cryptographic protocol that produces verified execution traces and an auditor that analyzes traces to detect and attribute attacks.
result: A single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, and exfiltrate up to 94% of prior tasks; their auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks with negligible latency overhead.
conclusion: The proposed cryptographic tracing and auditing approach effectively mitigates malicious behavior in decentralized multi-agent LLM systems while maintaining practical performance.

title: Side-Channel Analysis Of The Rp2350 Challenge 2
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bug bounty programs and community challenges have become an established mechanism to incentivize collective action to improve security. In essence, these can be considered as crowd-sourcing mechanisms where participants carry the risk twice over: performing the work in addition to having it officially accepted, which at times can be tied to unacceptable terms. Consequently, independent assessments and publications that are free from third party obligations remain important to highlight deficiencies in implementations of public significance. We consider the RP2350 side-channel analysis challenge and its hardened Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) implementation to be of reasonable importance to justify such an approach, especially so since the presented challenge remained unsolved for more than a year. In our paper, we present our analysis, demonstrating comprehensive leakage detection, plaintext dependence, and key extraction from the challenge implementation. Our work presents concerning weaknesses in the implementation that contradict the challenge authors' claims. We hope by openly sharing this analysis to motivate further public scrutiny.
tldr: The paper analyzes the RP2350 side-channel challenge and demonstrates leakage detection, plaintext dependence, and key extraction from its hardened AES implementation.
motivation: The authors argue that independent public scrutiny of bug bounty challenges is important, especially since the RP2350 side-channel challenge remained unsolved for over a year.
method: They perform side-channel analysis on the challenge's hardened AES implementation, including leakage detection, plaintext-dependence analysis, and key-recovery attempts.
result: The analysis reveals comprehensive leakage and enables key extraction, contradicting the challenge authors' security claims.
conclusion: The work highlights concerning weaknesses in the implementation and aims to motivate further public scrutiny of such security challenges.

title: A Gpu Interior-Point Solver With Macro-Element Condensation For Equilibrium-Based Plasticity
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equilibrium-based conic formulations of elastoplasticity and limit analysis provide statically admissible stress fields but generate large Newton systems whose sparse factorization limits three-dimensional computations. This work develops and analyzes a macro-element condensation tailored to the Newton systems arising from primal--dual interior-point methods. Exploiting four-tetrahedron macro-elements, the method eliminates stress directions and macro-internal traction-continuity multipliers, yielding reduced systems that can be solved using positive-definite factorizations, with estimated reductions of approximately \(4\times\) in dimension and structural nonzeros relative to stress-only elimination. The validity of this elimination is established through global and macro-local nonsingularity conditions. Local nonsingularity is independent of the yield criterion in elastoplasticity, whereas in limit analysis it holds directly for Rankine and is ensured for von Mises through trace-bound augmentation. Numerical results show that, relative to stress-only elimination, the proposed condensation achieves CPU speedups of up to approximately \(2\times\) and reduces peak linear-solver memory by up to \(66.5\%\). We further develop a CUDA Fortran implementation that exploits uniform macro-local blocks through batched routines and uses cuDSS for the reduced sparse solve. This implementation achieves speedups of up to \(13.5\times\) over its CPU counterpart and up to \(87.5\times\) over MOSEK, while successfully solving the largest tested 3D problems that exceed the device-memory capacity of the GPU solver CuClarabel. For elastoplasticity, we also propose a preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that reduces device-memory requirements relative to the direct GPU solver, at the expense of increased solution time.
tldr: A GPU-accelerated interior-point solver using macro-element condensation for equilibrium-based elastoplasticity and limit analysis in 3D solid mechanics.
motivation: Equilibrium-based conic formulations of elastoplasticity yield large Newton systems whose sparse factorization bottlenecks three-dimensional computations, motivating a dimension-reducing condensation strategy.
method: Four-tetrahedron macro-elements are used to eliminate stress directions and traction-continuity multipliers, giving positive-definite reduced systems, with nonsingularity conditions proved; a CUDA Fortran implementation uses batched routines and cuDSS, plus a preconditioned CG variant for elastoplasticity.
result: Dimension and nonzeros are reduced roughly 4x, CPU speedups reach ~2x with up to 66.5% lower peak memory; the GPU solver is up to 13.5x faster than its CPU version and 87.5x faster than MOSEK, solving problems beyond CuClarabel's memory capacity.
conclusion: Macro-element condensation makes equilibrium-based 3D plasticity solvers practical on GPUs, though the work lies entirely in computational solid mechanics and numerical optimization.

title: Reject And Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks For Generative Image Models
authors: Yihan Wang, Haochen Sun, Xi He, Yaoliang Yu, N. Asokan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.
tldr: Tripwire-WM is a forgery-evident watermarking framework for generative image models that commits image semantics to latent-noise magnitudes so forged watermarks are both rejected and reported.
motivation: Existing undetectable watermarking schemes such as SemBind resist forgery poorly and silently discard forged images without leaving evidence, allowing adversaries to falsely attribute harmful content to a model or make real photographs appear AI-generated.
method: The authors bind image semantics to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise—left unused by sign-based watermarks—via a distribution-preserving embedding built on pseudorandom-code watermarks and Gaussian Shading++, so a forgery carries a valid watermark whose commitment mismatches the content.
result: On MS-COCO, Tripwire-WM accepts no imprinting forgeries (vs. up to 55.0% for SemBind) and reports all of them, accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries (vs. 46.2%), and accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 1e-6 FPR while matching base-scheme robustness.
conclusion: Forgery-evident watermarking is achievable without sacrificing undetectability, providing both rejection and an auditable report of forgery attempts for generative image provenance.

title: Stability Bands For Feature Attribution: The Core, The Nucleolus And The Bargaining Set Of Explained-Variance Games
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation. We study feature attribution through the core, the nucleolus and the bargaining set of an explained-variance game, in which the worth of a set of features is the variance of the model's predictions that those features generate. For every feature we report a stability band (its range of shares over the core, or over the least core when the core is empty), with the nucleolus as distinguished point and a certificate that the allocation admits no justified objection. Three results organise the approach. First, for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, with pairwise Harsanyi dividends [MATH], so multicollinearity is what creates coalitional structure. Second, in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, the (least) core is point-symmetric around it, and the core is non-empty if and only if every cut of the interaction graph has non-negative weight. The Shapley value thus always lies in the prebargaining set, and stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. Third, for convex games the bands have a closed form and any allocation can be certified with one minimum cut. In a hedonic price model, the usual mean-SHAP explanation admits a justified objection by the coalition {Ratings, ROM, Battery}. In a gradient-boosting forecaster of retail orders the exact game has an empty core and strong higher-order interactions; the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares, and sparse third-order surrogates recover it where pairwise ones cannot.
tldr: The paper analyzes Shapley-value feature attributions through cooperative-game solution concepts such as the core, nucleolus, and bargaining set for explained-variance games.
motivation: Standard Shapley-based explanations report a single attribution per feature and do not indicate whether coalitions of features could contest the allocation, so the authors seek stability bands and coalitional stability guarantees.
method: They define an explained-variance cooperative game, study its 2-additive structure for linear models, derive core and least-core stability bands, and use the nucleolus and bargaining set to certify allocations, with applications to hedonic pricing and gradient-boosting forecasts.
result: For linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, and core non-emptiness is characterized by cuts of the interaction graph; in a hedonic price model a coalition can raise a justified objection, while in a retail-order forecaster the exact game has an empty core and higher-order interactions matter.
conclusion: Feature-attribution stability can be formalized via cooperative-game solution concepts, providing richer diagnostics than mean SHAP alone, but the work is outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.
tldr: LingSante MedGuard is a unified medical safety guardrail model that combines a medical guardrail teacher with six specialized capability experts to detect harmful, non-compliant, or unethical clinical AI responses.
motivation: As medical AI systems are deployed for consultation and clinical decision support, there is a need to identify harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic outputs by checking clinical claims against evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical rules.
method: The authors build a capability-enhanced guardrail via offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student responses, integrating a guardrail teacher and six medical capability experts, and introduce the MedGuardBench benchmark with 11 risk-detection subsets.
result: At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales the model achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, and the 4B model reaches 73.9% mean accuracy on MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation, with improved evidence consistency, source traceability, and rationale quality.
conclusion: The results support integrating specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based safety verification.

title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference For Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
authors: Sikha Pentyala, Steven Golob, Daniil Filienko, Ming-Chun Kao, Martine de Cock
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.
tldr: The paper presents a GPU-accelerated secure multiparty computation system for privacy-preserving drug-target interaction inference.
motivation: Drug-target interaction models need private inference because candidate drugs are valuable intellectual property, but secure deep-model inference is slow due to communication-heavy nonlinear operations and poor MPC-GPU mapping.
method: The authors co-design SlimDTA, a DTI model with fewer secret-drug nonlinear operations, and a GPU MPC framework using additive secret sharing for linear layers, function secret sharing for nonlinear layers, and a custom CUDA comparison kernel.
result: Their solution won Track III of iDASH 2026, achieving under 10 ms per prediction on average while matching plaintext model predictions within 0.02%.
conclusion: GPU-aware MPC protocol and model co-design can make two-party secure DTI inference practical, though the work is classical cryptography and machine learning rather than quantum information.

title: Lattice-ordered Spectral Systems For Morse Representations
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that Morse representations can be algebraically described by spectral systems, a notion introduced by B. Matschke for poset-filtered chain complexes. This provides an algebraic alternative to connection matrices and yields algebraic invariants via R-modules over an arbitrary ring R. This approach applies in particular to Conley index theory for semi-flows. We discuss the theory of spectral systems and, as an application to dynamical systems, explain the relation to R. Franzosa's theory of connection matrices. In this context we introduce the concept of a spectral net. In contrast to traditional spectral sequences, spectral nets over a lattice display a rich network of (higher) differentials. In the application to dynamical systems these differentials provide information about connecting orbits.
tldr: The paper develops lattice-ordered spectral systems as an algebraic framework for Morse representations and Conley index theory.
motivation: Morse representations and connection matrices are important in dynamical systems and topological invariants, but their algebraic description can be clarified using spectral systems.
method: The authors use spectral systems over poset-filtered chain complexes and R-modules to algebraically encode Morse representations, and introduce spectral nets over lattices.
result: Spectral systems provide an algebraic alternative to connection matrices and yield invariants via R-modules, with spectral nets exhibiting a network of higher differentials related to connecting orbits.
conclusion: The framework connects algebraic topology, Conley index theory, and dynamical systems, but has no direct relevance to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gaussian Quasi-Likelihood Estimation For Nonsynchronously Observed L\'evy Processes
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study parametric inference for a two-dimensional simple L\'evy process observed at high frequency over an expanding time horizon, where the two components are sampled in a possibly non-synchronous manner. Combining Gaussian quasi-likelihood estimation for L\'evy SDEs with the non-synchronous quasi-likelihood methodology, we construct a Gaussian-type quasi-likelihood based on the covariance structure of non-synchronous increments, and we prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting estimators. The convergence rates coincide with those in the synchronous setting, while the asymptotic variance depends essentially on the sampling design and becomes more complicated under non-synchronicity. To handle the different moment structure of pure-jump L\'evy processes, we introduce an additional convergence assumption and provide tractable sufficient conditions linked to the observation scheme. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators.
tldr: The paper develops Gaussian quasi-likelihood estimation for two-dimensional Lévy processes observed nonsynchronously at high frequency over an expanding horizon.
motivation: Parametric inference for high-frequency Lévy data is complicated when the two components are sampled at non-synchronous times, requiring adapted quasi-likelihood methods.
method: The authors combine Gaussian quasi-likelihood for Lévy SDEs with non-synchronous quasi-likelihood methodology, constructing a likelihood based on the covariance structure of non-synchronous increments and proving asymptotic properties.
result: Estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal with convergence rates matching the synchronous case, while the asymptotic variance depends on the sampling design and becomes more complex under non-synchronicity.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides tractable sufficient conditions for pure-jump Lévy processes and is illustrated via numerical experiments.

title: The Four-Element Theory Of Structure-Driven Methodology: A Methodological Shift From The Perspective Of Natural Science And Engineering Practice
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, fundamentally driven by the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm, rely on setting external objectives and iterative trial-and-error. When confronted with complex nonlinear problems containing noise and conflicting constraints, this paradigm inherently induces statistical smoothing and compromise, yielding black-box models that lack interpretability and out-of-distribution generalization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology, reconstructing the solving process into four irreversible stages: Deconstruction, Structure, Construction, and Solving. The method suspends a priori presuppositions to strip unit coupling, extracts rigid invariants inherent to the problem, constructs equivalent mappings anchored to these invariants, and executes the mapping directly to generate the solution. Evaluation metrics and experience are relegated to a posteriori verification. Demonstrated through cross-disciplinary practices including number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion, this methodology transcends the statistical fitting bottleneck. Structure-Driven and Objective-Driven methodologies are complementary: when structure is sufficient, solutions are directly constructed; when lacking, it degenerates into the OD path.
tldr: The paper proposes a Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology for solving complex nonlinear problems by deconstruction, structure extraction, construction, and solving, contrasting with optimization-driven AI.
motivation: Mainstream optimization-driven AI relies on external objectives and trial-and-error, producing black-box models that lack interpretability and out-of-distribution generalization on complex noisy problems.
method: The methodology suspends a priori assumptions, strips unit coupling, extracts rigid invariants, constructs equivalent mappings anchored to invariants, and directly executes mappings for solutions, with evaluation relegated to a posteriori verification.
result: Cross-disciplinary demonstrations in number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion suggest the approach can transcend statistical fitting bottlenecks, and it degenerates to optimization-driven methods when structure is insufficient.
conclusion: Structure-driven and objective-driven methodologies are complementary, with structure-driven solving offering direct construction when sufficient invariants are available.

title: A Decoupled Structure-preserving Scheme For Pressure-driven Multispecies Tumor Growth
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an Onsager-based scheme for an [MATH]-species pressure-driven reaction--cross-diffusion system with a common homeostatic pressure. The scheme uses a modified scalar energy structure to update the total density, followed by compatible updates of the individual species. The global nonlinear problem remains scalar, and the species densities sum exactly to the updated total density. We establish unique solvability and show that the scheme preserves species nonnegativity, the pressure bound and total-mass monotonicity and satisfies a discrete energy dissipation law without a time-step restriction. We further develop a predictor--corrector extension to improve temporal accuracy while retaining these structural properties. Numerical experiments verify the accuracy and structure-preserving properties of the proposed schemes and demonstrate their computational efficiency.
tldr: The paper proposes an Onsager-based, structure-preserving numerical scheme for a pressure-driven multispecies tumor growth reaction–cross-diffusion model.
motivation: Multispecies tumor growth models require numerical schemes that preserve key physical structures such as nonnegativity, mass conservation, pressure bounds, and energy dissipation.
method: The authors introduce a decoupled scheme using a modified scalar energy structure to update total density, followed by compatible species updates, plus a predictor–corrector extension for improved temporal accuracy.
result: They prove unique solvability and structural properties including species nonnegativity, pressure bounds, total-mass monotonicity, and a discrete energy dissipation law without time-step restrictions, supported by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The scheme is accurate, efficient, and structure-preserving for the targeted tumor growth system, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Self-Supervised Operator Learning For Channel Estimation In Fluid Antenna Systems
authors: Erqiang Tang, Zixin Wang, Wei Guo, Shenghui Song, Jun Zhang, Khaled B. Letaief
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluid antenna systems (FAS) have emerged as a promising technology for enhancing wireless communications through adaptive antenna repositioning. Recently, Fourier neural operators (FNOs) have shown strong potential for FAS channel estimation owing to their ability to learn resolution-invariant mappings and generalize across different port densities. However, existing operator learning approaches require densely sampled channel realizations as training labels, whereas a practical receiver only collects noisy pilot observations from a small subset of ports. This mismatch between training requirements and practical channel acquisition poses a major obstacle to deployment. To address this challenge, we develop a self-supervised framework that trains the FNO-based estimator directly from noisy sub-sampled pilots without any labeled channel fields. The proposed objective combines a pilot splitting strategy, which creates supervision at ports hidden from the model input, with a correction based on Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE) that eliminates the measurement noise bias. We prove that this objective admits the same minimum mean square error (MMSE) solution as the ideal supervised criterion. Since the loss relies solely on received pilots, the estimator can be continually adapted online on the live pilot stream. Simulation results show that the self-supervised FNO achieves accuracy comparable to supervised training, generalizes zero-shot to unseen port resolutions, and rapidly recovers from distribution shift via online adaptation.
tldr: This paper develops a self-supervised Fourier neural operator framework for channel estimation in fluid antenna systems using noisy sub-sampled pilots.
motivation: Existing operator-learning approaches for fluid antenna channel estimation require densely sampled labeled channel realizations, which are impractical because receivers only collect noisy pilot observations from a small subset of ports.
method: The authors train an FNO-based estimator directly from noisy sub-sampled pilots by combining a pilot-splitting strategy with a SURE-based noise-bias correction, and prove the objective shares the MMSE solution of the ideal supervised criterion.
result: Simulations show accuracy comparable to supervised training, zero-shot generalization to unseen port resolutions, and rapid recovery from distribution shift through online adaptation.
conclusion: Self-supervised operator learning enables practical, label-free channel estimation for fluid antenna systems and supports continual online adaptation on live pilot streams.

title: Proportional Representation For Almost-Solid Coalitions And The Proportional Veto Core For Rankings
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A proportional ranking should give groups of voters representation commensurate with their size at every prefix. Proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC) provides this guarantee to groups whose members rank the same set of candidates above all others. How much representation should a group receive when a few outside candidates disrupt that agreement? We extend the proportional veto core to rankings through candidatewise and setwise guarantees. We show that setwise veto protection is equivalent to robust Rank-PSC under reversal of both the voters' preferences and the collective ranking. Robust Rank-PSC extends representation guarantees to almost-solid coalitions at every prefix. Each distinct outside candidate that disrupts a coalition's agreement reduces its guaranteed representation by at most one, and this bound is tight. Using reverse-sequential variants of Ordered Phragm\'en and STV, we construct rankings satisfying robust Rank-PSC[MATH] in polynomial time. This stronger axiom preserves the guarantee after deleting any suffix of the collective ranking and restricting voters' preferences to the remaining candidates. Verifying robust Rank-PSC is coNP-complete, whereas verifying robust Rank-PSC[MATH] takes polynomial time. We also introduce Rank-Aligned PJR[MATH], which requires the first [MATH] candidates of the collective ranking to satisfy PJR[MATH] when each voter approves their top [MATH] candidates. We give a polynomial-time algorithm that meets this requirement simultaneously for every [MATH]. For fixed-size committees, the Expanding Approvals Rule guarantees Rank-PJR[MATH] but can violate robust PSC regardless of how ties are broken or payments are assigned. We give a modification that satisfies both guarantees for any prescribed committee size.
tldr: The paper studies proportional representation axioms for ranked voting outcomes, extending proportional veto core and Rank-PSC guarantees to almost-solid coalitions and providing polynomial-time construction and verification results.
motivation: Proportional ranking methods should give voter groups representation matching their size at every prefix, but existing solid-coalition guarantees break when a few outside candidates disrupt coalition agreement.
method: The authors formalize candidatewise and setwise veto guarantees for rankings, relate setwise veto protection to robust Rank-PSC under preference and ranking reversal, and use reverse-sequential Ordered Phragmén and STV variants to construct satisfying rankings.
result: They show robust Rank-PSC bounds representation loss by at most one per distinct disrupting outside candidate, construct rankings satisfying robust Rank-PSC[MATH] in polynomial time, prove verification complexity separations, and introduce Rank-Aligned PJR[MATH] with a simultaneous polynomial-time algorithm.
conclusion: The work strengthens proportional ranking axioms and algorithms, but it belongs to computational social choice and voting theory, not to any of the listed quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems research directions.

title: A Branch-free Three-dimensional Ghost-cell Immersed Boundary Method With Direction-averaged Extrapolation Kernels
authors: Itsuki Takarabe, Ryuto Saeki, Koji Fukagata
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ghost-cell immersed boundary methods impose the wall boundary condition on a Cartesian grid by assigning values to the grid points just inside the body, the ghost points. A common approach reconstructs the ghost value from an image point, which requires a wall normal for every ghost point. Special treatments are also often required where the interpolation stencil leaves the fluid region, e.g., near thin, concave or highly curved parts of complex bodies. We present a ghost-cell method that needs neither wall normals nor image points. Instead of a single extrapolation direction, the method uses all fluid nodes within 2.5 grid spacings of a ghost point that satisfy a simple geometric condition. The ghost value is obtained as the average of one-dimensional linear extrapolations from these nodes through the wall crossings of the connecting segments. The weights depend only on the geometry and are computed offline as one kernel on a [MATH] stencil per ghost point. The boundary treatment at run time is thus an explicit, branch-free weighted sum. For the flows around a sphere and the Stanford Bunny, a self-convergence study shows approximately second-order convergence of the velocity in the [MATH] and [MATH] norms. The maximum difference also decreases at second order for the sphere but more slowly for the Stanford Bunny, where it is observed at a few nodes next to the wall. The drag coefficient of the sphere at Reynolds numbers of 25--200 agrees with a previous study within 2.4% for 32 grid cells per diameter and 0.4% for 64. For the Stanford Bunny at a Reynolds number of 100, the force coefficients agree with a body-fitted solution within 1% for 64 grid cells per reference length, without any geometry-specific treatment. Although no pressure condition is imposed on the wall, the pressure field is smooth and consistent with the body-fitted solution.
tldr: The paper introduces a branch-free ghost-cell immersed boundary method for Cartesian-grid CFD that uses direction-averaged linear extrapolation kernels to impose no-slip wall conditions without wall normals or image points.
motivation: Standard ghost-cell immersed boundary methods require wall normals and image points for every ghost node and need special treatment where interpolation stencils leave the fluid, complicating implementation for thin, concave, or highly curved geometries.
method: Ghost values are computed as geometry-weighted averages of one-dimensional linear extrapolations from all fluid nodes within 2.5 grid spacings that satisfy a simple geometric condition; the weights are precomputed offline into a single stencil kernel per ghost point, yielding a runtime boundary treatment that is an explicit branch-free weighted sum.
result: Self-convergence studies for flow past a sphere and the Stanford Bunny show approximately second-order velocity convergence in L1 and L-infinity norms; sphere drag coefficients at Re = 25-200 agree with prior work within 2.4% (32 cells/diameter) and 0.4% (64 cells), and Bunny force coefficients at Re = 100 agree with body-fitted solutions within 1%.
conclusion: The method achieves body-fitted-level accuracy on complex geometries without geometry-specific treatment, wall normals, or image points, and produces smooth, consistent pressure fields despite imposing no explicit pressure wall condition.

title: Geometry, Local Minimax Risk, And The Limits Of Sample Average Approximation In Linear Stochastic Optimization
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how the local geometry of a linear stochastic optimization problem determines its statistical difficulty, measured by expected decision regret. The optimal local rate is governed by how fast the support function of the feasible set grows away from its linearization at the true mean; depending on the instance, it can be [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or a non-power rate, and sample average approximation (SAA) attains these rates in a Gaussian mean model. At smooth instances, SAA also attains the classical sharp local minimax constant. We then allow the data distribution to vary in a Kullback--Leibler (KL) ball of radius proportional to [MATH] around a reference distribution [MATH]. The exact local minimax limit of this benchmark, which may depend on [MATH], coincides with that of a Gaussian model whose local parameter set is the covariance ellipsoid of [MATH]. A simple coordinatewise truncated SAA rule, which does not use [MATH], attains the minimax rate, and at smooth instances its constant matches the minimax constant as the neighborhood radius grows. Ordinary SAA, in contrast, can have strictly suboptimal worst-case expected regret when the local rate is fast relative to the tails of [MATH], because rare tail events then dominate the expectation. The results delineate when SAA is sharply optimal, rate-optimal, or statistically suboptimal, and quantify the local price of distributional robustness.
tldr: The paper characterizes how local geometry of linear stochastic optimization problems governs minimax decision regret and delineates when sample average approximation (SAA) is sharply optimal, rate-optimal, or suboptimal, including under KL-ball distributional uncertainty.
motivation: Practitioners need to know when SAA — the default data-driven approach in stochastic optimization — achieves statistically optimal regret, and how local problem geometry and distributional robustness affect achievable rates and constants.
method: Derives local minimax lower bounds tied to the growth rate of the feasible set's support function, establishes matching Gaussian-model benchmarks, and analyzes a coordinatewise truncated SAA rule under KL-ball ambiguity sets.
result: Local rates can be power-law or non-power depending on geometry; SAA attains them in Gaussian models and matches sharp constants at smooth instances, but plain SAA can be strictly suboptimal when local rates are fast relative to distribution tails.
conclusion: The work precisely maps when SAA is statistically optimal versus suboptimal and quantifies the local price of distributional robustness, offering guidance for robust decision rules in stochastic optimization.

title: Rank And Rel In Strata Of Abelian Differentials
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every invariant subvariety M in a genus g stratum H(k_1,...,k_n) of Abelian differentials satisfies rank(M) <= rel(M) + 1 + sum_i (k_i - 1). In particular, every invariant subvariety with rel zero in a principal stratum is a Teichm\"uller curve. Combined with work of Eskin, Filip and Wright, this implies that each principal stratum contains only finitely many nonarithmetic Teichm\"uller curves. If rank(M) < g, we also show that rank(M) + rel(M) <= g - 1 + n/2.
tldr: The paper proves new inequalities relating the rank and rel invariants of invariant subvarieties in strata of Abelian differentials, with consequences for the finiteness of nonarithmetic Teichmüller curves in principal strata.
motivation: Rank and rel are the two fundamental invariants controlling the geometry and dynamics of invariant subvarieties (orbit closures) in moduli space, and understanding their constraints has been a central open problem since the work of Eskin–Filip–Wright.
method: The author derives algebraic-geometric inequalities bounding rank in terms of rel and the stratum's singularity orders, and further bounds rank + rel when rank is below the genus.
result: It is shown that rank(M) <= rel(M) + 1 + sum_i(k_i - 1) for every invariant subvariety M in H(k_1,...,k_n), that rel-zero subvarieties in principal strata are Teichmüller curves, and that principal strata contain only finitely many nonarithmetic Teichmüller curves.
conclusion: These results tighten the structural constraints on orbit closures of Abelian differentials and yield finiteness statements for nonarithmetic Teichmüller curves, contributing to the classification program in Teichmüller dynamics.

title: A Modified Quasi-Newton Method For Unconstrained Optimization With Nonpositive Curvature Detection And Structured Complexity
authors: Farhad Rahbarnia, Dominique Monnet, Dominique Orban
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the convergence, worst-case complexity, and implementation of R2N, a modified quasi-Newton method for large-scale unconstrained smooth optimization. At each iteration, we compute a step that approximately minimizes the sum of a quadratic model of the objective with an adaptive quadratic regularization, and that results in sufficient decrease. The objective is only assumed to be [MATH], although second derivatives may be used if they are available. The implementation features a broad range of step-computation strategies, from sparse factorization to matrix-free Krylov methods, that satisfy global convergence requirements. When detected, directions of nonpositive curvature are exploited. Our analysis allows unbounded model Hessians, provided they satisfy a mild growth condition. We derive a worst-case evaluation complexity bound that separates the progress made along positive- and nonpositive-curvature directions. By forcing the regularization parameter to vanish near isolated local minimizers, we obtain superlinear local convergence. The implementation specializes naturally to nonlinear least-squares problems. We provide a modular Julia implementation, and use it in a numerical study on the CUTEst test set that assesses the treatment of nonpositive curvature, the subproblem solver, the update of the regularization parameter, and direct versus iterative subproblem solves. An Armijo-Goldstein line search along nonpositive-curvature directions, MINRES-QLP as subproblem solver, and a regularization parameter driven to zero near a solution form our recommended configuration. With exact second derivatives, R2N is competitive with a trust-region method, solving slightly more problems with fewer objective and gradient evaluations. With convex models, the trust-region method performs as well or better.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes R2N, a modified quasi-Newton method for large-scale unconstrained smooth optimization with nonpositive curvature detection and structured worst-case complexity.
motivation: Large-scale smooth optimization requires robust methods that handle nonconvexity, including nonpositive curvature, while retaining global convergence and favorable local convergence properties.
method: The authors analyze a regularized quasi-Newton step, derive worst-case evaluation complexity separating positive- and nonpositive-curvature directions, and implement modular Julia strategies including MINRES-QLP and Armijo-Goldstein line search.
result: The method achieves superlinear local convergence when regularization vanishes near isolated minimizers and is competitive with a trust-region method on CUTEst, especially with exact second derivatives.
conclusion: R2N provides a practical and theoretically grounded quasi-Newton framework for nonconvex unconstrained optimization, though it is outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems.

title: The Scaled Dirichlet Distribution: Lauricella Representations And Estimation
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive explicit expressions for the mixed moments of the scaled Dirichlet distribution in terms of the Lauricella hypergeometric function of type [MATH]. The relationship with Carlson's multivariate [MATH]-function is stated, and the convergence conditions required for the series derivation are made explicit. The general expressions yield means, second moments and covariances, with Gauss and Appell hypergeometric representations in the bivariate and trivariate cases. Method-of-moments and maximum-likelihood formulations are presented, together with simulation summaries and an illustrative comparison of scaled Dirichlet and ordinary Dirichlet fits to compositional futures-return data.
tldr: The paper derives closed-form mixed moments of the scaled Dirichlet distribution via Lauricella hypergeometric functions and develops method-of-moments and maximum-likelihood estimation procedures.
motivation: The scaled Dirichlet distribution is a flexible compositional-data model, but its moment structure and estimation theory remain less developed than those of the ordinary Dirichlet distribution.
method: Explicit series representations of mixed moments are derived in terms of Lauricella hypergeometric functions, linked to Carlson's multivariate function, with stated convergence conditions and Gauss/Appell specializations for the bivariate and trivariate cases.
result: Means, second moments and covariances are obtained in closed form, and moment-based and likelihood-based estimators are presented with simulation studies and a fit comparison on compositional futures-return data.
conclusion: The hypergeometric framework provides a tractable analytical handle on scaled Dirichlet moments and a practical alternative to the ordinary Dirichlet for compositional modelling.

title: Kakutani Equivalence Of Higher Rank Unipotent Abelian Actions I
authors: Adam Kanigowski, Philipp Kunde, Kurt Vinhage, Daren Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Kakutani equivalence of higher-rank abelian unipotent actions. We construct a Kakutani invariant for general [MATH]-actions and establish a quantitative vanishing criterion. By this criterion, we prove that ergodic abelian horocyclic actions on finite-volume quotients of connected semisimple Lie groups are loosely Kronecker. We also include a proof of the Abramov entropy formula for time changes of Rn-actions, following the strategy developed by Nadler.
tldr: The paper constructs a Kakutani invariant for higher-rank abelian unipotent actions and uses it to prove that ergodic abelian horocyclic actions on finite-volume quotients of semisimple Lie groups are loosely Kronecker.
motivation: Kakutani equivalence and time-change invariants for higher-rank abelian actions are poorly understood compared to the Z-action case, and a quantitative vanishing criterion would enable classification of such parabolic actions.
method: The authors build a general Kakutani invariant for R^n-actions, derive a quantitative vanishing criterion for it, and apply this to horocyclic actions on quotients of semisimple Lie groups; they also give a proof of the Abramov entropy formula for time changes of R^n-actions following Nadler's strategy.
result: Ergodic abelian horocyclic actions on finite-volume quotients of connected semisimple Lie groups are shown to be loosely Kronecker, and the Abramov entropy formula for time changes of R^n-actions is established.
conclusion: The work provides new invariants and criteria for Kakutani equivalence in higher-rank settings, extending classification results to horocyclic abelian actions.

title: Computing Optimal Non-stationary Policies For The Probabilistic Reach-Avoid Problems
authors: Saber Omidi, Momotaz Begum, Marek Petrik, Se Young Yoon
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop and analyze an algorithm for computing optimal non-stationary policies for probabilistic reach-avoid problems. The objective in probabilistic reach-avoid problems is to maximize the probability of reaching a goal without visiting predefined avoid states. Prior work has focused on computing optimal stationary reach-avoid policies. Stationary policies use the same action distribution whenever a given state is visited. This paper shows that stationary reach-avoid policies may be suboptimal and non-stationary policies may outperform them in reach probability by a margin arbitrarily close to one. To compute optimal non-stationary policies, we reduce the reach-avoid problem to a constrained average-reward Markov decision problem and propose an algorithm to compute lottery-based policies from a standard linear program formulation. We prove that the lottery-based policies are optimal and show that they are simple to compute, analyze, interpret, and implement. The numerical experiments confirm that the lottery-based policies can outperform state-of-the-art stationary policies even in complex domains.
tldr: The paper develops an algorithm for computing optimal non-stationary policies in probabilistic reach-avoid problems by reducing them to constrained average-reward Markov decision processes.
motivation: Prior work focused on stationary reach-avoid policies, but the authors show these can be arbitrarily suboptimal compared with non-stationary policies.
method: The reach-avoid problem is reduced to a constrained average-reward MDP, and optimal lottery-based policies are computed via a standard linear program formulation.
result: The authors prove lottery-based policies are optimal and show numerically that they can outperform state-of-the-art stationary policies in complex domains.
conclusion: Non-stationary lottery-based policies provide a principled and practical approach for probabilistic reach-avoid planning, with strong theoretical optimality guarantees.

title: Sharp Box-dimension Bounds For Fractional Integrals Under Unequal H\"older And anti-H\"older Exponents
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] and [MATH]. Graph box dimensions are studied for fractional integrals of functions satisfying an [MATH]-Holder upper bound on increments and an [MATH]-anti-H \"lder lower bound on oscillation on a nondegenerate subinterval. For the Riemann--Liouville integral, the following inequalities hold: \[ \max\{1,2-H-\sigma H/h\} &\le\lbdim\G(I_{0+}^{\sigma}f,[0,1])\\ &\le\ubdim\G(I_{0+}^{\sigma}f,[0,1]) \le\max\{1,2-h-\sigma\}. \] The lower bound is obtained by balancing the truncation error of a Marchaud inverse against the oscillation of the input. For each [MATH], a single sparse tent construction attains it for all [MATH]. The same bounds and their optimality are established for Hadamard integrals on compact intervals bounded away from zero and for left- and right-sided Liouville--Weyl integrals under explicit weighted tail conditions. Zero-mean periodic Weyl integrals with conditionally convergent tails are treated separately. For Hadamard integrals the bounds are transferred by a bi-Lipschitz logarithmic change of variables. For Weyl integrals the transfer relies on invariance of graph box dimensions under continuous perturbations of bounded variation. Local hypotheses and point-dependent anti-H\"older constants are also treated. The exact linear dimension law is recovered for equal exponents, whereas unequal exponents allow a strictly greater loss of graph dimension.
tldr: A pure analysis paper establishing sharp box-dimension bounds for Riemann–Liouville, Hadamard, and Liouville–Weyl fractional integrals of functions obeying unequal Hölder upper and anti-Hölder lower conditions.
motivation: Graph box dimensions of fractional integrals are known only under symmetric Hölder assumptions; the authors aim to characterize the dimension loss when the upper Hölder exponent and the lower anti-Hölder exponent of the input differ.
method: Truncation error of a Marchaud-type fractional inverse is balanced against the input's oscillatory anti-Hölder lower bound to obtain matching upper and lower dimension bounds, with sparse tent constructions; results are transferred to Hadamard and Weyl integrals via a bi-Lipschitz logarithmic change of variables and invariance under bounded-variation perturbations.
result: The graph box dimension of the Riemann–Liouville integral is bracketed between max{1, 2−H−σH/h} and max{1, 2−h−σ}, with the bounds sharp for every exponent pair; the classical linear dimension law is recovered only for equal exponents.
conclusion: Unequal Hölder/anti-Hölder exponents permit a strictly greater loss of graph dimension than the equal-exponent case, and the framework extends to Hadamard, Liouville–Weyl, and zero-mean periodic Weyl integrals.

title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery In Php Web Applications
authors: Xinyi Wang, Yeting Li, Shizhe Cui, Jiaming Guo, Qin Mai, Yecheng Sun, Hengyu Yang, Yujie Sun, Huina Chao, Yang Xiao, Feng Li, Wei Huo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain. We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection.
