It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses. We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).
tldr: ChainAgent is an LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies directly in PHP source code.
motivation: High-impact PHP attacks typically chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors, but existing tools analyze flaws in isolation or assume known attack components, leaving chain-relevant unknowns undiscovered.
method: Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world exploit chains, the framework models vulnerabilities and functional gadgets via preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects, and uses an evolving exploit graph to drive backward and forward source-code searches.
result: Against Codex on 15 PHP applications across three LLM backends, ChainAgent achieves 42.02%–44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and up to 4.4x more correct dependency edges; on 30 real-world applications it finds 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine yielding RCE.
conclusion: Goal-directed, chain-aware LLM agent analysis substantially improves discovery of exploitable vulnerability chains in web applications compared to general-purpose coding agents.

title: ToolPulse: Side-Channel Eavesdropping On Tool-Using Llm Agents
authors: Zihao Dan, Jinyu Zhang, Jinzhao Lian, Yun Chen, Shinan Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that translate user requests into sequences of local tool invocations. While prior cache-based side-channel attacks target the locally deployed models, they typically require the adversary to share model-related components or hardware resources with the victim's inference process. These assumptions do not apply to the predominant agentic settings, in which commercial LLMs execute on vendor-controlled infrastructure. We show that agentic execution exposes a more practical attack surface: although inference remains remote, tools are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries. In this paper, we first systematically evaluate Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe for monitoring agentic tool invocations. Our evaluation across three hardware platforms shows that Flush+Reload enables accurate, real-time tool monitoring, whereas Prime+Probe, despite supporting cross-VM attacks, incurs prohibitive monitoring overhead and suffers from cache-set aliasing. We present ToolPulse, a cache-based side-channel eavesdropping framework against tool-using agents. We first design the Tool Recovery Attack to reconstruct an agent's tool-execution workflow. We evaluate the Tool Recovery Attack on 11 LLMs across Codex and Claude Code. It consistently reconstructs tool workflows, with the lowest F1 score exceeding 93%. We further demonstrate two attack scenarios enabled by the recovered traces. Task Profiling Attack infers user intent across two Terminal-Bench task categories and the Trigger Localization Attack identifies sensitive tool calls in encryption/decryption and model training/inference workloads. Even under substantial system noise on a server shared by approximately 20 users, both Task Profiling Attack and Trigger Localization Attack maintain high accuracy.
tldr: ToolPulse is a cache-based side-channel framework (Flush+Reload/Prime+Probe) that eavesdrops on tool invocations executed locally by remote tool-using LLM agents, recovering tool workflows and inferring user intent.
motivation: Prior cache side-channel attacks on LLMs assume the adversary shares model components or hardware with the victim's inference, which fails in agentic settings where inference is remote on vendor infrastructure while tools run on the user's machine using shared system libraries.
method: The authors systematically evaluate Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe across three hardware platforms, then build ToolPulse, comprising a Tool Recovery Attack reconstructing tool-execution workflows, plus a Task Profiling Attack and a Trigger Localization Attack exploiting the recovered traces.
result: Tool Recovery achieves F1 above 93% on 11 LLMs across Codex and Claude Code; task profiling and trigger localization retain high accuracy even under heavy noise on a server shared by ~20 users.
conclusion: Agentic LLM execution exposes a practical local side-channel surface that leaks user intent and sensitive tool calls, motivating new defenses for tool-using agents.

title: Compact MaxSAT Encodings For Balanced Waiting In B2b Meeting Scheduling
authors: Tuyen van Kieu, Long Duc Nguyen, Minh Duc Dang Vu, Khanh van To
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Business-to-business (B2B) meeting schedules can leave participants with long and uneven waits. Earlier break-based B2B models count interruptions without measuring their duration. Our earlier work minimizes the range of participant idle totals, but a minimum range can still leave long waits. We study lexicographic optimization of idle range, maximum idle, and total idle, in that order. Waiting is measured in empty slots between a participant's first and last meetings. Balance compares idle totals among participants requesting at least two meetings. Using weighted maximum satisfiability (MaxSAT), we prove preservation of feasible schedules, objective costs, and priorities. Compact-Base retains our earlier feasibility encoding; Compact-Objective adds objective-specific representations. We compare both with Direct, an independent implementation based on the 2022 MaxSAT model. Encoding comparisons use three repetitions per encoding-objective-instance combination on 226 variants of 20 base instances. Schedule-quality comparisons use break, range, and lexicographic objectives with the same encoding and feasible set. Across nine objective-dataset comparisons, Compact-Objective had the lowest median clause count and lower median peak memory than Direct. Runtime rankings changed in comparisons with the same solver build and computing environment. On 84 instances solved optimally under all three quality objectives, selected lexicographic schedules preserved the optimal idle range. Compared with selected range-only schedules, maximum idle decreased on 11 instances and total idle on 56. On 68 instances also solved optimally under range-then-total optimization, the selected schedules matched the three-tier criterion values. Compact-Base supplied the larger clause reduction relative to Direct; Compact-Objective reduced clauses further.
tldr: This paper develops compact weighted MaxSAT encodings for lexicographic optimization of participant idle time in B2B meeting scheduling, showing reduced clause counts and memory versus a direct MaxSAT baseline.
motivation: Existing break-based B2B scheduling models count interruptions without measuring their duration, and minimizing only the idle range can still leave participants with long waits, motivating a lexicographic treatment of idle range, maximum idle, and total idle.
method: Two encodings (Compact-Base reusing an earlier feasibility encoding, and Compact-Objective adding objective-specific representations) are compared against a Direct implementation derived from a 2022 MaxSAT model, benchmarked on 226 variants of 20 base instances with three repetitions per encoding-objective-instance combination.
result: Compact-Objective achieved the lowest median clause count and lower median peak memory in nine objective-dataset comparisons, though runtime rankings varied; lexicographic schedules preserved optimal idle range while reducing maximum idle on 11 and total idle on 56 instances.
conclusion: Compact MaxSAT encodings enable effective lexicographic balancing of waiting times in B2B meeting scheduling, with Compact-Base and Compact-Objective offering progressively larger clause reductions over the direct formulation.

title: Azowl AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance For Deployed Agent Applications
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.
tldr: AZOWL AgentOps is an operational governance layer for deployed LLM agent applications, linking task delegation to sender authority, assigned runners, approvals, and result evidence.
motivation: Deploying autonomous agents in business workflows raises questions of who authorized a task, which runner executed it, and whether safeguards (read-only profiles, approval gates) were respected, so shared governance across human and agent senders is needed.
method: The authors compare AZOWL components against a configured LangGraph application across 28 synthetic runs in four paired pilots, using isolated component tests, mock providers for protected writes, and two deployed inventory/GRC audit traces with receipt hashing.
result: Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and made zero writes when an approved delivery address changed; AZOWL's scope gate re-requested approval on the same task, and a 0.6.57 deployed run was traced end-to-end with matching local and central artifact hashes.
conclusion: Task-scoped governance with stable task identifiers and evidence receipts is feasible for deployed agents, though protected-write evaluations relied on mock providers and small synthetic pilots.

title: Uniqueness, Proximity, And Scaling In Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes. The algorithm first computes equilibria of associated integer-splittable games, in which demands are allocated in multiples of a common packet size. For arbitrary polymatroid bases, no polynomial-time algorithm for these discrete equilibria was previously known. We provide such an algorithm and use progressively finer packets to recover the continuous equilibrium exactly. Our proof uses the multiple-exchange theorem of Oki and Schwarcz (2025) to obtain two exchange matchings that yield equilibrium proximity under changes of packet sizes and ranks, independently of cost coefficients. We then bound the matching deficiency caused by rank changes and construct compatible submodular rank roundings. Together these give a polynomial-time packet-halving algorithm using polynomially many submodular-function minimizations and exact rational arithmetic. The analysis rests on a uniqueness theorem of independent interest: for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, we prove uniqueness of equilibria, resolving a previously open problem.
tldr: The paper presents a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games, together with a new uniqueness theorem for equilibria with convex, strictly increasing latencies.
motivation: Exact equilibrium computation for atomic splittable congestion games with general polymatroid bases was open; no polynomial-time algorithm was known even for the associated integer-splittable discretization.
method: The authors compute equilibria of integer-splittable games with progressively finer packet sizes, prove exchange-matching-based proximity bounds independent of cost coefficients via the multiple-exchange theorem, bound matching deficiency under rank changes, and construct compatible submodular rank roundings, yielding a packet-halving algorithm using exact rational arithmetic and submodular minimization.
result: A polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation is obtained, and uniqueness of equilibria is proven for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks with continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, resolving a previously open problem.
conclusion: The work closes open questions on equilibrium computation and uniqueness in polymatroid congestion games, but it lies entirely within classical algorithmic game theory and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Raven: A Self-RAG Based Agent For Threat Classification And Response
authors: Pironti Francesco Aurelio, Arena Luigi, Blefari Francesco, Lupinacci Matteo, Romeo Francesco, Furfaro Angelo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.
tldr: RAVEN is an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework that automates the initial triage and classification of security alerts in Security Operations Centers, with analyst-in-the-loop refinement and context-aware remediation suggestions.
motivation: SOC analysts face overwhelming volumes of alerts that require manual inspection, making triage slow and inconsistent; the authors aim to automate the early stages of alert investigation.
method: The system uses a Self-Reflective RAG approach to classify security events, grounding responses in enterprise infrastructure knowledge, and supports interactive refinement via analyst queries; it is evaluated on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) plus a qualitative case study.
result: An early-stage prototype is presented with preliminary classification results on the curated payload datasets and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; evaluation on IDS alerts and a user study remain ongoing.
conclusion: RAVEN shows promise as an LLM-agent assistant for SOC alert triage, but the work is in progress and lacks full empirical validation.

title: Question, Then Affirm: Restoring Commitment Does Not Restore Refusal
authors: Haoyang Xu, Qirui Wang, Liuwan Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We find that safeguards for image generation can be bypassed without changing what a message says. A sign stating a harmful proposition is blocked, but the same proposition phrased as a question and followed by a check mark is generated, even though the resulting image endorses the original claim. On a 300-case challenge set, gpt-image-2 returns images for 43.3% of question-affirmation requests versus 16.3% of direct statements, with 41.3% versus 15.3% of cases yielding images that endorse the original proposition. We define this as Deferred Semantic Commitment (DSC): commitment is withdrawn by the question and restored by a separate element, while safety behavior follows only the withdrawal. To investigate why, we study an open-weight language model and find that re-endorsement only partially reverses the refusal-related change introduced by questioning. These findings reveal a mismatch between recovered meaning and refusal behavior, motivating safeguards that assess the completed message rather than its individual elements.
tldr: The paper identifies a jailbreak pattern, Deferred Semantic Commitment (DSC), in which harmfulness safeguards for image generation can be bypassed by phrasing a harmful claim as a question followed by an affirmation mark.
motivation: Safety filters typically evaluate individual message elements rather than the completed message's meaning, leaving a gap that adversarial phrasings may exploit.
method: The authors construct a 300-case challenge set of harmful propositions phrased as direct statements versus question-plus-checkmark forms, measure gpt-image-2's image generation and endorsement rates, and probe an open-weight language model's internal refusal-related representations.
result: gpt-image-2 returned images for 43.3% of question-affirmation requests versus 16.3% of direct statements, with 41.3% versus 15.3% producing endorsing images; re-endorsement only partially reverses the refusal-related representational change in the open-weight model.
conclusion: Recovered meaning does not restore refusal behavior, motivating safeguards that assess the completed message rather than its individual components.

title: AI-Native Industrial Control Systems: An Agent Architecture For The Control System Lifecycle
authors: Lisi Liu, Ang Zhou, Chuan Pang, Feng Gao, Shengkai Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial control systems increasingly use AI for perception, control, and engineering, while available control functions and execution environments are typically established in advance. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control system in which collaborating agents determine the capabilities required by a task, construct the control application, and prepare its execution environment. System-level agents coordinate device-level agents within configured resource and permission constraints. A physical sorting workstation illustrates two forms of adaptation. In the first case, controller and robot agents construct a sorting application on a prescribed Raspberry Pi target. In the second, a camera agent adds inspection on an edge node, and the controller associates inspection results with downstream pickup decisions. A subsequent revision enables selective sorting using the same agents and deployment arrangement. The trials demonstrate the feasibility of task-driven construction and evolution on the workstation. Commissioning also reveals limitations in the traceability of design decisions, adherence to delegated responsibilities, diagnostic reasoning, and verification of physical behavior.
tldr: The paper proposes an AI-native industrial control system in which collaborating LLM-based agents determine required capabilities, build control applications, and prepare execution environments, demonstrated on a physical sorting workstation.
motivation: Industrial control systems increasingly incorporate AI for perception, control, and engineering, yet their available control functions and execution environments are typically fixed in advance, limiting task-driven adaptation.
method: A hierarchical agent architecture is proposed in which system-level agents coordinate device-level agents under configured resource and permission constraints, then instantiated on a Raspberry Pi-based sorting workstation with controller, robot, and camera agents, including a revised selective-sorting configuration.
result: The trials show feasibility of task-driven construction and evolution of control applications, while commissioning exposes limitations in traceability of design decisions, adherence to delegated responsibilities, diagnostic reasoning, and verification of physical behavior.
conclusion: Task-driven agent-based construction of industrial control applications is feasible at the workstation scale, but trustworthiness requirements such as traceability, responsibility adherence, and physical verification remain open challenges.

title: The Partial Trace Functor On Soergel Bimodules In Type $\mathbb{B}$
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We write down some observations about the partial trace functor between the categories of Soergel bimodules of type [MATH] and [MATH] for future reference. In particular, we observe that, like in type [MATH], the partial trace sends Soergel bimodules to a semi-infinite [MATH]-graded sum of Soergel bimodules.
tldr: The paper records observations on the partial trace functor between categories of type B Soergel bimodules.
motivation: The author aims to document structural behavior of the partial trace functor for Soergel bimodules in type B, analogous to known results in type A.
method: The work uses categorical and representation-theoretic techniques for Soergel bimodules, specifically analyzing how the partial trace functor acts on objects and grading.
result: The main observation is that the partial trace sends Soergel bimodules to a semi-infinite graded sum of Soergel bimodules, mirroring the type A behavior.
conclusion: These observations are intended as a reference for future work on partial trace functors and Soergel bimodules in type B.

title: Pointwise Minmax Representations For Total Variation Denoising On Graphs
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Total variation denoising (TVD) is a fundamental method in image denoising, signal processing, and nonparametric regression. We establish exact pointwise minmax/maxmin representations for TVD on arbitrary finite graphs, extending recent one-dimensional results. Under squared loss, fitted values are expressed through corrected local averages over nested connected vertex sets. The correction is a signed boundary count: edges leaving the inner set contribute +1 if they remain within the outer set and -1 otherwise. To the best of our knowledge, this representation is new even for two-dimensional TVD. We show that Brunk's classical minmax formulas for isotonic regression on every finite directed acyclic graph arise as special cases of our graph TVD representation. The exact reduction proceeds through asymmetric TVD and nearly isotonic regression, which coincides with isotonic regression above a finite penalty threshold. We further extend the representations to arbitrary finite separable convex losses, assuming coercivity of the full objective, but without requiring differentiability or strict convexity. For nonunique solutions, the possible fitted values at each coordinate form a compact interval. Its lower and upper endpoints admit maxmin and minmax representations, respectively, through scalar local optimization problems and are attained simultaneously at all coordinates by two extremal solutions. This yields exact representations for quantile TVD on arbitrary graphs and unifies TVD, nearly isotonic regression, and isotonic regression within a single pointwise framework for general separable convex losses.
tldr: The paper establishes exact pointwise minmax/maxmin representations for total variation denoising on arbitrary finite graphs and extends them to separable convex losses.
motivation: Total variation denoising is a fundamental method in image denoising, signal processing, and nonparametric regression, but exact pointwise representations were previously limited to one-dimensional settings.
method: The authors derive representations via corrected local averages over nested connected vertex sets, using signed boundary counts, and connect graph TVD to asymmetric TVD, nearly isotonic regression, and Brunk's isotonic regression minmax formulas.
result: They obtain new exact representations valid for arbitrary finite graphs and separable convex losses, including interval-valued fitted values for nonunique solutions with maxmin/minmax endpoints attained by extremal solutions.
conclusion: The work unifies TVD, nearly isotonic regression, and isotonic regression in a single pointwise framework for general separable convex losses, with exact representations even in two dimensions.

title: Covering Location Optimization At Gpu Speed
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale covering location optimization often involves NP-hard combinatorial problems that pose substantial computational challenges in urban facility planning. This paper proposes a GPU-accelerated parallel search framework for the maximal covering location problem, combining device-resident multi-trajectory exploration with lightweight CPU-side coordination. Exploiting the structure of one-swap moves, exact incremental gains are evaluated through sparse coverage representations and tiled CUDA kernels. A hierarchical reduction identifies the best exchange without materializing the full swap-gain matrix, while GPU-resident destroy-and-repair and elite-guided restarts balance intensification and diversification. Computational experiments on nine real-world urban configurations demonstrate consistent improvements over GRASP, achieving a mean relative gap of 0.029\% against published best-known solutions (BKS) and reaching BKS in 50 of 90 independent runs. On the largest urban benchmark, Kings, with 7,730 candidate locations and a budget of 50 facilities, the proposed method reaches BKS in all ten runs using a consumer-grade NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti GPU, requiring only 45.2 seconds on average to obtain its final incumbent, compared with 99.5 seconds reported for AILS-PR in a high-performance computing cluster environment. The source code and benchmark reproduction scripts are publicly available at [URL].
tldr: A GPU-accelerated parallel search framework solves the maximal covering location problem, matching best-known solutions on real-world urban benchmarks in tens of seconds on consumer hardware.
motivation: Large-scale maximal covering location problems are NP-hard combinatorial optimization tasks whose computational cost hinders urban facility planning at realistic scale.
method: The authors combine device-resident multi-trajectory search with lightweight CPU coordination, evaluating exact one-swap incremental gains via sparse coverage representations and tiled CUDA kernels, plus hierarchical reduction, GPU-resident destroy-and-repair, and elite-guided restarts.
result: Across nine real-world urban configurations the method attains a mean gap of 0.029% to published best-known solutions, hitting BKS in 50 of 90 runs and in all ten runs on the largest benchmark (7,730 locations) in 45.2 s on a GTX 1660 Ti.
conclusion: Commodity GPUs can deliver high-performance-computing-level results for large covering location optimization, making such solvers accessible for practical planning.

title: Criteria For Memory-induced Blow-up In Distributed Delay Differential Equations
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the conditions under which solutions to distributed delay differential equations describing memory accumulation and forgetting blow up in finite time. It provides criteria for memory-induced blow-up, which means finite-time blow-up of the delayed equation while the corresponding non-delayed equation, obtained in a certain limit, has global solutions. In the author's previous work, memory-induced blow-up was shown for specific nonlinearities by means of Poincar\'e-type compactification, but a general theory was not established. Here, the two-dimensional ODE system derived by the linear chain trick is rewritten as an orbit equation, and a comparison theorem and an Osgood-type integral condition are applied to obtain a blow-up criterion based on the existence of a subsolution. This characterizes the nonlinearities for which memory-induced blow-up occurs. This paper also gives a necessary condition in a special case, a global existence condition based on a supersolution, and a systematic method for constructing subsolutions for separable nonlinearities. These results recover the author's previous results and are illustrated through several examples.
tldr: The paper derives criteria for finite-time blow-up in distributed delay differential equations caused by memory effects, using an orbit-equation and subsolution comparison approach.
motivation: Previous work showed memory-induced blow-up only for specific nonlinearities, so the author seeks a general theory characterizing when delayed memory accumulation causes finite-time blow-up while the corresponding non-delayed system has global solutions.
method: The linear chain trick rewrites the distributed delay equation as a two-dimensional ODE system, which is then expressed as an orbit equation; comparison theorems and an Osgood-type integral condition yield a blow-up criterion via subsolutions.
result: The paper obtains a general subsolution-based blow-up criterion, a necessary condition in a special case, a global existence condition via supersolutions, and a systematic method for constructing subsolutions for separable nonlinearities.
conclusion: The framework characterizes nonlinearities leading to memory-induced blow-up and recovers earlier specific results, but it is a pure applied-mathematics contribution with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Ties At The Top: A Point-in-Time Comparison Of Cvss And Epss At A Fixed Budget
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organizations must decide which vulnerabilities warrant further analysis and protective action when the volume of published vulnerabilities exceeds their analytical capacity. We present a methodology for comparing vulnerability-prioritization strategies under an explicit resource constraint, represented by a fixed number of CVEs selected from a common eligible population. We apply this methodology to the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS). For CVEs published in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) from 17 March to 31 December 2025 and from 1 January to 31 March 2026 (Q1), we reconstruct each CVE's scores and status 30 days after NVD publication, using archived source data. Each cohort has one ranking per strategy at a 5% budget. Positives are CVEs added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog within 180 days after their decision day. The catalog is maintained by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). EPSS captures 16 of 40 positives in 2025, versus 5 for CVSS; alternative selections among tied CVEs cannot raise CVSS capture above 9. In Q1, CVSS captures 4 of 11 and EPSS 3, but tie-breaking can reverse this ordering. The score alone leaves most of each CVSS list undecided: the tie-breaking rule allocates 1,678 of 1,919 CVSS places in 2025 and 589 of 758 in Q1 among CVEs tied at score 9.8. Most chosen CVSS scores come from non-NVD providers; disabling those scores reduces CVSS capture from 5 to 1 in 2025 and from 4 to 0 in Q1. A fixed-budget comparison should therefore report its decision cutoff, eligible population, score provenance, and tie-breaking rule.
tldr: A point-in-time, fixed-budget comparison of CVSS and EPSS vulnerability-prioritization strategies using NVD and CISA KEV data.
motivation: Organizations cannot analyze every published vulnerability, so they need evidence about which prioritization scoring system best selects vulnerabilities that are actually exploited.
method: Reconstructs CVSS and EPSS scores and status 30 days after NVD publication for 2025 and Q1 2026 cohorts, selects the top 5% of CVEs under each strategy, and counts how many selected CVEs enter the CISA KEV catalog within 180 days, including analysis of ties and score provenance.
result: EPSS captured 16 of 40 positives in 2025 versus 5 for CVSS (and at most 9 with tie-breaking), while CVSS captured 4 of 11 versus 3 for EPSS in Q1 with a reversal possible under tie-breaking; most CVSS places are decided by ties at 9.8 and rely on non-NVD providers.
conclusion: Fixed-budget comparisons of vulnerability prioritization must report the decision cutoff, eligible population, score provenance, and tie-breaking rule.

title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning With Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
authors: Syed Ahzaz Shah, Evan Bramblett, H\'eber H. Arcolezi, Chen Gong, Qianqian Tong, Xiaochen Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows. In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.
tldr: PriTabICL is a differentially private tabular in-context learning framework that synthesizes cluster-wise demonstrations to preserve prediction-relevant relationships.
motivation: Tabular in-context learning relies on labeled demonstrations that may contain sensitive information, while standard DP noise can distort feature-label relationships and degrade predictive performance.
method: The paper partitions records into DP clusters, synthesizes each cluster independently with a prediction-relevant feature-target workload, and routes inference queries to an appropriate DP cluster for demonstration sampling.
result: On four real-world datasets, PriTabICL-PrivSyn improves over global PrivSyn in 8 of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings.
conclusion: Cluster-wise DP synthesis with task-aligned workloads can better preserve heterogeneous local structure for private tabular in-context learning than global synthesis.

title: Living Off The Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models For Post-Exploitation
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely.We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.
tldr: The paper demonstrates that browser-embedded local language models such as Gemini Nano in Chrome can be repurposed by attackers as on-device post-exploitation engines.
motivation: Vendor-shipped, locally running LLMs are invisible to network monitoring and already present on endpoints, creating a new living-off-the-land attack surface that has not been characterized.
method: The authors drive the Gemini model from the host using only OS-native interpreters, bypass the one-time user-activation check via a simulated click, and measure its capabilities for credential identification, PII detection, image classification, and tool calling.
result: They combine these capabilities into an end-to-end simulated cyber operation: extracting a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration without user interaction.
conclusion: Browser-embedded models constitute a practical, signed, and hard-to-detect post-exploitation capability, motivating new defensive considerations for locally deployed LLMs.

title: User Perceptions Of Deceptive In-Vehicle Infotainment User Interfaces
authors: Pedram Mohajeransari (clemson University), Iwinosa Aideyan (clemson University), Anna Galeano (clemson University), Arjun Arunasalam (florida International University), Bart Knijnenburg (clemson University), Richard Brooks (clemson University), Mert D. Pes\'e
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern vehicles collect extensive data about drivers, passengers, and vehicle use, with privacy and consent decisions increasingly mediated through infotainment software. Although dark patterns have been widely studied in web, mobile, and e-commerce interfaces, little is known about how they appear in automotive infotainment systems or how users perceive them. We study this problem through Android Automotive OS (AAOS), conducting a three-phase empirical analysis. First, 26 HCI and privacy annotators audit four OEM AAOS emulators (Honda, Volvo, GM, and Polestar), documenting 17 dark-pattern types across 65 observations. Second, a user study with 100 participants compares OEM-specific implementations of five dark patterns across GMC, Honda, and Volvo, finding that implementation choices affect user perceptions. Third, an independent study with 49 participants compares automotive and e-commerce dark-pattern clips before and after a brief tutorial, showing that automotive's initial rating advantage largely collapses after instruction. Together, the studies identify a sophistication paradox: subtler dark patterns are less likely to trigger user suspicion and may therefore be harder to identify. These findings indicate that oversight should evaluate not just the presence but also the specific implementation of dark patterns.
tldr: A three-phase empirical HCI study of deceptive 'dark pattern' designs in Android Automotive OS infotainment interfaces and how users perceive them.
motivation: Modern vehicles collect extensive driver and passenger data while privacy and consent decisions are mediated through infotainment software, yet dark patterns have been studied mainly in web, mobile, and e-commerce contexts, leaving automotive interfaces unexplored.
method: The authors conduct an expert audit of four OEM AAOS emulators (26 annotators), a 100-participant user study comparing five dark patterns across GMC, Honda, and Volvo implementations, and a 49-participant study comparing automotive versus e-commerce dark-pattern clips before and after a tutorial.
result: Implementation choices measurably affect user perception, and automotive dark patterns' initial rating advantage over e-commerce largely collapses after brief instruction; subtler dark patterns evade suspicion, revealing a 'sophistication paradox'.
conclusion: Oversight of automotive privacy interfaces must evaluate not only the presence but the specific implementation of dark patterns, since subtle designs are hardest for users to recognize.

title: Trace-5g: Trust-Aware Runtime Attestation And Continuous Enforcement For 5g User Equipment
authors: Al Nahian Bin Emran, Rajendra Paudyal, Rajendra Upadhyay, Arupjyoti Bhuyan, Duminda Wijesekera
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The standard 5G Authentication and Key Agreement protocol (5G-AKA) authenticates subscriber credentials but does not verify the integrity of user equipment (UE). Existing literature includes admission-time device-certificate authentication and Trusted Platform Module (TPM)-based measured-boot attestation, which can additionally verify that the UE presents enrolled device credentials and boots into an approved state. However, these checks do not reveal whether harmful unauthorized software is executed after admission. We present TRACE-5G, which continuously verifies the UE's runtime software state and uses the resulting trust state to control network access. TRACE-5G retains the pre-admission certificate and boot checks, and in addition places the admitted UE in restricted connectivity while runtime integrity is verified. Linux Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) records runtime software measurements, TPM PCR (Platform Configuration Register) cryptographically accumulates them, and Keylime, a remote-attestation framework, repeatedly evaluates TPM and IMA evidence against enrolled references. A Trusted result grants full access on the existing PDU session, but an Untrusted result withholds or removes full access and causes network deregistration. We implement TRACE-5G on an srsRAN/Open5GS testbed with a hardware TPM2.0 UE and core-side firewall enforcement. Across ten trusted trials, Level 2 access was established in 9--12s. Across ten untrusted trials, promotion was consistently withheld; in a representative trace, restrictive policy was applied within 5ms of the Untrusted decision and UE-context release completed within 1.670s. TRACE-5G extends UE trust beyond admission without any modification of the standardized 5G protocols.
tldr: TRACE-5G adds continuous TPM/IMA-based runtime attestation to 5G UE access control, restricting connectivity until trust is verified and revoking access on untrusted evidence.
motivation: Standard 5G-AKA authenticates subscriber credentials but does not verify UE runtime software integrity after admission, leaving a gap for malicious software execution.
method: The system combines Linux IMA runtime measurements, TPM PCR accumulation, Keylime remote attestation, and core-side firewall enforcement on an srsRAN/Open5GS testbed with a hardware TPM2.0 UE.
result: Trusted trials established Level 2 access in 9-12 s; untrusted trials consistently withheld promotion, with restrictive policy applied within 5 ms and UE-context release completed in 1.670 s in a representative trace.
conclusion: TRACE-5G extends UE trust beyond admission time without modifying standardized 5G protocols, but it is a classical 5G security/attestation contribution unrelated to quantum information science.

title: On The Monitorability Of Linear-time Timed Logics
authors: Mouloud Amara, Mohammed Aristide Foughali, Giovanni Bernardi, Adrian Francalanza, Nicanora Ordo\~no Wallig
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In [10], we solved the monitorability problem for Tlin , a new expressive (linear-time) timed mu-calculus that we proposed. We showed that Tlin is strictly more expressive than MTL, the de facto timed extension of the well-known LTL. Moreover, we identified MTlin , the largest monitorable fragment of Tlin. The maximality of MTlin was proven modulo an expressive monitoring framework called Mon, yet under the assumption of reactivity. Our work in [10] was the first to solve the monitorability problem for such an expressive timed logic, and its theoretical results were accompanied with compilers (i) from MTL to Tlin and (ii) from Tlin formulae to monitors. This paper is an extension of [10] with the following new contributions. First, we generalise the maximality results to arbitrary monitors, which include both reactive and non-reactive monitors. Second, we extend the expressiveness results of Tlin . We completely revise the embedding of MTL into Tlin : we show that the syntax of MTL given in [10] was incomplete, and provide a new compiler from MTL, under its standard syntax with the strict Until operator and negation over arbitrary formulae, into Tlin . In passing, we demonstrate that Tlin is closed under complement and provide a fully syntactic complementation procedure. Moreover, we prove that Tlin is strictly more expressive than TPTL, a popular timed logic more expressive than MTL, and develop an automatic embedding from TPTL to Tlin . This gives Tlin and the machinery around it the power of a unified framework to reason on the monitorability of linear-time timed logics. Accordingly, we identify important monitorable fragments for both MTL and TPTL.
tldr: This paper extends prior work on monitorability for Tlin, an expressive linear-time timed mu-calculus, generalizing maximality results to arbitrary monitors and revising its expressiveness relations to MTL and TPTL.
motivation: Monitorability of timed logics is central to runtime verification, and prior results for the expressive timed mu-calculus Tlin were proven only under a reactivity assumption, leaving the general case open.
method: The authors generalize the maximality proof of the monitorable fragment MTlin to arbitrary (reactive and non-reactive) monitors, provide a fully syntactic complementation procedure for Tlin, and construct new compilers embedding standard MTL and TPTL into Tlin.
result: Tlin is shown to be closed under complement and strictly more expressive than TPTL, the earlier MTL embedding is corrected, and important monitorable fragments of MTL and TPTL are identified.
conclusion: Tlin and its surrounding machinery form a unified framework for reasoning about monitorability of linear-time timed logics, yielding concrete monitorable fragments for MTL and TPTL.

title: Hardening JavaScript Programs Against LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection
authors: Zhenhao Tian, Jintong Yu, Jingwei Feng, Jianwei Zhuge, Penghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.25718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: JavaScript programs are often distributed as source code, so attackers can analyze them for vulnerabilities. LLM-based vulnerability detection agents now make this analysis much easier. To mitigate this emerging threat, we present AntiAgent, a defense that lets developers harden their programs against such detection agents. AntiAgent transforms a program before release to impede an agent's analysis. To find effective transformations, AntiAgent evolves a corpus of programs with known vulnerabilities and traces how a detection agent analyzes each evolved version. It keeps the versions on which the agent misses or misreports the vulnerability and extracts their transformations into reusable rules. To protect a new program, AntiAgent carefully divides the task between an LLM and the rules, so that the transformations adapt to the program while preserving its semantics. We evaluate AntiAgent on real-world JavaScript applications against four detection agents, including Claude Code and Codex. AntiAgent reduces the number of vulnerabilities that each agent detects by 52.0-60.7%, outperforming the conventional obfuscator JS-Obfuscator and the LLM-based transformation method FPA on every agent. The transformed programs pass all project tests, indicating that AntiAgent preserves the original program semantics. The transformation rules also remain effective on vulnerability types absent from the corpus and on programs written in another language like Python.
tldr: AntiAgent is a defense that transforms JavaScript source code to evade LLM-based vulnerability detection agents while preserving program semantics.
motivation: JavaScript is typically shipped as source, so LLM-powered vulnerability detection agents make it easier for attackers to find exploitable flaws, motivating a proactive hardening defense.
method: The authors evolve a corpus of vulnerable programs, trace how detection agents analyze each variant, keep evasions that cause missed or misreported vulnerabilities, and distill them into reusable transformation rules applied via an LLM-rule split that preserves semantics.
result: AntiAgent reduces detected vulnerabilities by 52.0-60.7% against four agents (including Claude Code and Codex), outperforming JS-Obfuscator and FPA, while passing all project tests and generalizing to unseen vulnerability types and to Python.
conclusion: Program transformation can meaningfully degrade LLM-based vulnerability detection without breaking functionality, though the work is purely software-security engineering.
